# Semantic Logger - Complete Documentation

> Semantic Logger is a high-performance, asynchronous structured logging framework for Ruby and Rails.

This file concatenates every page of https://logger.reidmorrison.com for consumption by AI assistants.
It is generated from the markdown sources in docs/ by `bundle exec rake llms_full`; do not edit it directly.
A per-page index is available at https://logger.reidmorrison.com/llms.txt


---

<!-- source: docs/index.md -->

## What is Semantic Logger?

Semantic Logger is a high-performance, asynchronous structured logging framework
for Ruby and Rails.

It does two things that ordinary loggers do not:

1. **It logs structured data, not just strings.** Along with the usual text message you can
   attach a payload (any Hash), an exception, a duration, metrics, and tags. That data is
   preserved all the way to the destination, so it stays searchable instead of being flattened
   into a line of text.
2. **It logs asynchronously.** Log events are placed on an in-memory queue and written to their
   destinations by a separate background thread. Your application is not blocked while logs are
   written to disk, a database, or a remote service.

If you are using Rails, use the companion gem
[rails_semantic_logger](https://github.com/reidmorrison/rails_semantic_logger), which replaces
the Rails logger automatically. See the [Rails guide](rails.html).

## Why use it?

### The problem with traditional logging

With the standard Ruby logger you eventually end up building messages by hand:

~~~ruby
logger.info("Queried users table in #{duration} ms, with a result code of #{result}")
~~~

That reads fine for a human, but to a machine it is just a string. To answer a question like
"show me every query that took longer than 100 ms" you have to write fragile regular expressions
against your log files, and every developer formats their messages slightly differently.

### The Semantic Logger way

Log the message and the data separately:

~~~ruby
logger.info("Queried users table",
  duration: duration,
  result:   result,
  table:    "users",
  action:   "query")
~~~

Now the same event is still readable by a human, but a machine can index `duration`, `result`,
`table`, and `action` as real fields. Send it to a JSON file, Elasticsearch, or Splunk and you can
search, filter, and build dashboards on those fields directly, no log parsing required.

### Reasons developers choose Semantic Logger

* **Fast.** Logging happens on a background thread, so even logging thousands of lines per second
  does not slow your application down. See [how it works](#how-it-works) below.
* **Structured.** Every log entry can carry a payload, exception, duration, metrics, and tags
  without losing that structure.
* **Human and machine readable at the same time.** Colorized text for developers, JSON for your
  log aggregator, written from the same log call.
* **Many destinations at once.** Write to a file, the screen, and a remote service simultaneously,
  each with its own log level and format. See [Appenders](appenders.html).
* **A familiar API.** It supports the standard `debug`/`info`/`warn`/`error`/`fatal` API, so
  existing code and other gems keep working. You mostly just change how the logger is created.
* **Built for production.** Per-class log levels, change the log level of a running process with a
  [signal](operations.html#linux-signals), tagged logging for tracing requests across threads, automatic exception
  capture, and [metrics](metrics.html) for dashboards.

## Quick start

Install the gem:

~~~bash
gem install semantic_logger
~~~

Or add it to your `Gemfile`:

~~~ruby
gem "semantic_logger"
~~~

Configure it once when your application starts, then log:

~~~ruby
require "semantic_logger"

# Log :info and above. Use :trace, :debug, :info, :warn, :error, or :fatal.
SemanticLogger.default_level = :info

# Send log output to the screen using the colorized formatter.
SemanticLogger.add_appender(io: $stdout, formatter: :color)

# Create a logger for the current class. The class name is added to every message.
logger = SemanticLogger["MyApp"]

logger.info("Application started")
~~~

That is the whole setup. The [Programmer's Guide](api.html) covers the full logging API.

## A tour of the features

The examples below assume you already have a `logger` from `SemanticLogger["MyApp"]`.

#### Log a message with structured data

~~~ruby
logger.error("Outbound call failed", result: :failed, reason_code: -10)
~~~

#### Log an exception

Pass the exception directly. The class, message, and backtrace are all captured, including any
nested "caused by" exceptions.

~~~ruby
begin
  # ... code that may raise
rescue => exception
  logger.error("Import failed", exception)
end
~~~

#### Only evaluate expensive messages when needed

Pass a block. It runs only when the log level is active, so it is skipped entirely in production
when the level is higher.

~~~ruby
logger.debug { "Processed a total of #{records.sum(&:size)} bytes" }
~~~

#### Measure how long something takes

The message is written when the block completes, together with its duration. If the block raises,
the exception is logged with the duration and then re-raised.

~~~ruby
logger.measure_info("Called external interface") do
  # Code to call the external service ...
end
~~~

#### Tag a block of related log entries

Every log entry inside the block carries the tags, which is invaluable for tracing one request
across many classes and threads.

~~~ruby
SemanticLogger.tagged(user: "jbloggs", request_id: "abc123") do
  logger.info("Hello World")
  logger.debug("More detail")
end
~~~

#### Name your threads

So concurrent log entries are easy to tell apart.

~~~ruby
Thread.current.name = "worker-1"
~~~

## How it works

Every logger forwards its log events to a single, shared background thread through an in-memory
queue. That thread writes each event to every registered appender (destination) in turn. Because
the writing happens off to the side, the thread that called `logger.info` returns immediately.

~~~mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph callers["Application threads"]
    direction TB
    A["OrderProcessor<br/>logger.info"]
    B["PaymentGateway<br/>logger.measure_info"]
    C["Rails<br/>logger.error"]
  end

  Q["In-memory queue<br/>max_queue_size: 10,000"]
  P(["Processor<br/>one background thread"])

  subgraph appenders["Appenders"]
    direction TB
    D["Screen"]
    E["File"]
    F["Elasticsearch"]
    G["Sentry"]
  end

  A -->|"enqueue, return"| Q
  B --> Q
  C --> Q
  Q --> P
  P --> D
  P --> E
  P --> F
  P --> G
~~~

This design is why Semantic Logger is both fast and thread safe: log calls from hundreds of
concurrent threads simply enqueue events, and each appender writes them out sequentially in the
correct order. For the rare cases where you want logging to happen inline on the calling thread,
see [Synchronous Operation](operations.html#synchronous-operation).

This design is also tunable for production workloads. The in-memory queue is capped by default
(blocking when full so that no log message is lost), but it can instead drop messages to protect
application availability, give a slow appender its own thread, retry transient appender failures,
and be monitored at runtime. See
[Performance and reliability tuning](operations.html#performance-and-reliability-tuning) in the
Configuration guide.

### Ruby Support

For the complete list of supported Ruby versions, see
the [Testing file](https://github.com/reidmorrison/semantic_logger/blob/main/.github/workflows/ci.yml).

## Programming Guide

This guide covers the logging API: how to get a logger, and everything you can do with it. It builds
up from the simplest log call to more advanced features further down, so you can read it top to
bottom or jump to the part you need.

It assumes Semantic Logger is already installed with at least one appender (a destination such as the
screen or a file). If not, start with the [quick start](index.html#quick-start), then come back here.
For configuring the library itself (log levels, formatters, destinations), see
[Configuration](config.html).

Every example below uses a `logger` obtained in Step 1.

## Step 1: Get a logger

Create one logger per class, passing the class itself:

~~~ruby
logger = SemanticLogger[MyClass]
~~~

When there is no class, for example in a script, pass a name instead:

~~~ruby
logger = SemanticLogger["MyApp"]
~~~

The class or name you supply is attached to every entry that logger writes, so entries from different
parts of the application stay easy to tell apart. Use one logger per class so each entry identifies
where it came from.

### The Loggable mixin (recommended)

Rather than creating a logger by hand in every class, include `SemanticLogger::Loggable`. It adds a
`logger` method to both the class and its instances, already named for the class:

~~~ruby
class Supplier
  include SemanticLogger::Loggable

  def self.some_class_method
    logger.debug("Accessible from class methods")
  end

  def call_supplier
    logger.debug("Accessible from instance methods")
  end
end
~~~

Every entry is identified as coming from `Supplier`:

~~~
2012-08-30 15:37:29.474 I [48308:main] Supplier -- Accessible from instance methods
~~~

A module can include `SemanticLogger::Loggable` too. The module gets a `logger` of its own, and its
instance methods get a `logger` in any class that includes the module, whether or not that class
includes `SemanticLogger::Loggable`:

~~~ruby
module Pricing
  include SemanticLogger::Loggable

  def price(amount)
    logger.info("Pricing", amount: amount)
  end
end

class Order
  include Pricing
end

Order.new.price(10)
~~~

The entry is identified as coming from `Order`, the class that called `price`. When that class has a
class level `logger`, such as one from `SemanticLogger::Loggable`, the module's methods use it instead.
When the class itself defines a `logger` instance method, they use that.

By default `SemanticLogger[...]` returns a brand new logger on each call. To share a single logger
per class instead, enable [logger caching](config.html#caching-loggers).

## Step 2: Log a message

Semantic Logger supports the standard Ruby and Rails logger API, so existing code keeps working:

~~~ruby
logger.info("Hello World")
~~~

There is one method per level. The levels, from the most detail to the least, are:

    :trace  :debug  :info  :warn  :error  :fatal

~~~ruby
logger.trace("Low level detail, such as data sent over a socket")
logger.debug("Information to aid problem determination")
logger.info("Something normal happened, such as a request received")
logger.warn("Something unexpected, but handled")
logger.error("An error occurred during processing")
logger.fatal("Something really bad happened")
~~~

The active level acts as a threshold. At the default of `:info`, the `info`, `warn`, `error`, and
`fatal` calls are written while `debug` and `trace` are skipped. `:trace` is the most detailed level,
useful for tracing low level calls such as data exchanged with an external service. Setting the
global default level, and changing it at runtime, is covered in
[Configuration](config.html#default-log-level).

To check whether a level is active (for example before doing expensive work):

~~~ruby
logger.info? # => true when :info and above are being logged
~~~

## Step 3: Add structured data

This is what sets Semantic Logger apart. Instead of building a sentence by hand, pass the data as a
Hash "payload" after the message:

~~~ruby
# Traditional logging bakes the data into a string:
logger.info("Queried users in #{duration}ms, result #{result}")

# Semantic Logger keeps the message and the data separate:
logger.info("Queried users", duration: duration, result: result, table: "users")
~~~

The message stays readable for a human, and the payload stays machine readable: a JSON, MongoDB, or
Elasticsearch appender indexes `duration`, `result`, and `table` as real fields, so you can search
and build dashboards on them without parsing log text. The fields that make up an entry are listed in
[Log Event](log.html).

## Step 4: Log an exception

Pass a Ruby exception as the second argument. Its class, message, and backtrace are all captured:

~~~ruby
begin
  # ... code that may raise
rescue => exception
  logger.error("Outbound call failed", exception)
end
~~~

To log a payload and an exception together, pass both:

~~~ruby
logger.error("Outbound call failed", {result: :failed}, exception)
~~~

## Step 5: Skip expensive messages with a block

When building the message is itself expensive, pass a block instead of a string. The block runs only
when the level is active, so it costs nothing when that level is turned off (for example in
production):

~~~ruby
logger.debug { "Processed #{records.sum(&:size)} bytes across #{records.size} records" }
~~~

### The full call signature

Putting the pieces together, every level method accepts:

~~~ruby
logger.info(message, payload_or_exception = nil, exception = nil, &block)
~~~

- `message`: the text message. Optional only when a block is supplied.
- `payload_or_exception`: an optional Hash payload, or a Ruby exception.
- `exception`: an optional exception, used when you are also passing a payload.
- `&block`: evaluated only when the level is active; its return value becomes the message.

The same call can also be written as a single Hash, which is handy when assembling fields
programmatically:

~~~ruby
logger.debug(message: "Calling Supplier", payload: {request: "update", user: "Jack"})

# Log a complete exception
logger.error(message: "Calling Supplier", exception: exception)

# Attach a duration of 100ms
logger.error(message: "Calling Supplier", duration: 100)

# Attach a metric (see Step 6)
logger.error(message: "Calling Supplier", metric: "Supplier/inquiry", metric_amount: 21)

# Attach a backtrace of your own, an Array of Strings, instead of the logger's call stack
logger.warn(message: "Open redirect detected", backtrace: redirect_stack)

# Say where the entry was logged, or that it has no such place (see call_site_level)
logger.debug(message: "Order Load", duration: 0.4, call_site: query_location)
logger.info(message: "Started GET /orders", call_site: false)
~~~

In both forms, a key such as `duration` or `exception` is only used as an argument when its value is
valid for it; otherwise it is logged as part of the payload. Any other keys supplied alongside
`payload:` are merged into it, without overwriting its own values. When the Hash holds untrusted
data, see [Logging untrusted hashes](security.html#logging-untrusted-hashes).

A block can return the same Hash, but it never replaces an argument the entry already has. That
includes the backtrace that an entry captures when its level is at or above
`SemanticLogger.backtrace_level`, so to attach a backtrace of your own, pass `backtrace:` with the
call rather than returning it from the block.

## Step 6: Measure how long something takes

It is good practice to "measure everything" in production, so that when things slow down it is
obvious where the time is going. Wrap the code in a `measure_*` call:

~~~ruby
logger.measure_info("Called external interface") do
  # Code to call the external service ...
end
~~~

The entry is written once the block completes, and includes the duration:

~~~
2012-08-30 15:37:29.474 I [48308:script/rails] (5.2ms) Rails -- Called external interface
~~~

If the block raises, the exception is logged at the same level along with the duration, then re-raised
unchanged. There is a measure method for every level:

~~~ruby
logger.measure_trace / measure_debug / measure_info / measure_warn / measure_error / measure_fatal
~~~

Or supply the level dynamically as the first argument:

~~~ruby
logger.measure(:info, "Request received") do
  # ...
end
~~~

### Only log when it is slow (elastic logging)

Pass `min_duration` (in milliseconds) to log only when the block runs longer than the threshold.
This surfaces slow calls without the noise of the fast ones:

~~~ruby
logger.measure_warn("Called memcache", min_duration: 3) do
  # Usually fast; only logged when it takes longer than 3 ms
end
~~~

### Record a metric

Attach a `metric` name to feed dashboards. Once a metric appender is added, the duration is
recorded as a metric at every level, and whether or not `min_duration` is met, while the log entry
still follows the log level. See [Metrics](metrics.html):

~~~ruby
logger.measure_info("Called external interface", metric: "Supplier/inquiry") do
  # ...
end
~~~

To time code for a metric without logging it, use `logger.time` instead:

~~~ruby
logger.time("supplier.inquiry") { supplier.inquiry }
~~~

Add `dimensions` to break the metric down, such as by supplier. See
[Dimensions](metrics.html#dimensions):

~~~ruby
logger.measure_info("Called external interface",
                    metric:     "Supplier/inquiry",
                    dimensions: {supplier: "acme"}) do
  # ...
end
~~~

### Supply the duration yourself

When you already have a duration, log it without a block. This keeps the duration as structured data
rather than embedding it in the message text:

~~~ruby
duration = Time.now - start_time
logger.measure_info("Called external interface", duration: duration)
~~~

Either a block or `:duration` must be supplied on every measure call.

### All measure options

The second argument to a measure call is a Hash of options:

- `:min_duration` [Float]: only log if the block takes longer than this many milliseconds. Default
  `0.0` (always log).
- `:metric` [String]: record the duration as a metric with this name, once a metric appender is
  added, at every level. It must be in the options before the call to be timed below the level.
- `:dimensions` [Hash]: key/value labels that break the metric down, such as `{supplier: "acme"}`.
- `:payload` [Hash]: an optional payload to log with the entry.
- `:exception` [Exception]: an exception to log along with the duration.
- `:duration` [Float]: the duration in ms, used when no block is supplied (then it is mandatory; with
  a block it is ignored).
- `:log_exception` [Symbol]: how to report an exception raised in the block. `:full` logs the class,
  message, and backtrace of the exception and of each exception that caused it; `:partial` adds their
  classes and messages to the log message, without backtraces; `:none` does not log it. Default
  `:partial`. With `:partial`, a cause's message is left out when it is empty, is its class name, or
  is already in the log message, as when the exception that wraps it copied it into its own:

  ```
  Rendering -- Exception: ActionDispatch::Http::MimeNegotiation::InvalidType: "foo/bar" is not a valid MIME type -- Cause: Mime::Type::InvalidMimeType
  ```
- `:on_exception_level` [Symbol]: if an exception is raised, raise the log level to this level.
- `:silence` [Symbol]: the level to silence other log messages to within the block (current fiber
  only).
- `:call_site` [Thread::Backtrace::Location|SemanticLogger::CallSite|false]: where the entry was
  logged, or `false` for none. See
  [Recording where each entry was logged](config.html#recording-where-each-entry-was-logged).

An option with a value that is not valid for it, such as a non-numeric `:min_duration` or an unknown
level, is ignored and its default is used. Other keys in the Hash are not logged; pass the data to
log as `:payload`.

Putting several together:

~~~ruby
logger.measure_info("Called external interface",
                    log_exception: :full,
                    min_duration:  100,
                    metric:        "Custom/Supplier/process") do
  # Code to call the external service ...
end
~~~

## Step 7: Tag related entries

In a concurrent application it is invaluable to find every entry that belongs to one request or job.
`tagged` adds tags to every entry logged inside its block:

~~~ruby
tracking_number = "15354128"

SemanticLogger.tagged(tracking_number) do
  logger.debug("Hello World") # this entry carries the tracking_number tag
end
~~~

Prefer named tags. They are clearer as a system grows, and easier to filter and alert on in a
centralized logging system:

~~~ruby
SemanticLogger.tagged(user: "Jack", zip_code: 12345) do
  logger.debug("Hello World") # carries user and zip_code
end
~~~

Tags belong to the current fiber: each thread has its own, and so does each fiber of a fiber
scheduler such as [Async](https://github.com/socketry/async), which runs every request of a
[Falcon](https://github.com/socketry/falcon) server in its own fiber. So concurrent requests never
see each other's tags, and a thread, fiber, or Async task started inside the block does not have
them either. Hand them over explicitly, as shown next.

### Hand tags to another thread or fiber

`SemanticLogger.context` returns a frozen snapshot of the current tags, named tags, and
[silence](#silence-noisy-code) level. `SemanticLogger.with_context` applies it in another thread or
fiber for the duration of a block:

~~~ruby
SemanticLogger.tagged(request_id: request.uuid) do
  context = SemanticLogger.context

  Thread.new do
    SemanticLogger.with_context(context) do
      logger.info("Generating report") # carries request_id
    end
  end
end
~~~

The same works for an Async task or a thread pool:

~~~ruby
context = SemanticLogger.context
barrier = Async::Barrier.new
urls.each do |url|
  barrier.async do
    SemanticLogger.with_context(context) { fetch(url) }
  end
end
barrier.wait

context = SemanticLogger.context
pool.post do
  SemanticLogger.with_context(context) { process(item) }
end
~~~

Within the block, the thread or fiber has exactly the tags, named tags, and silence level of the
snapshot, in place of its own, which come back when the block exits. Add more tags inside the block
as usual. The snapshot does not carry levels set with a logger's `with_level`, which, like Ruby's own
`Logger#with_level`, apply only to the fiber that set them.

Tags are not handed over automatically because a long-lived thread, such as a thread pool's worker,
would otherwise keep the tags of whichever request happened to start it, and log them for every
later request it serves.

### Bind tags to one logger (child loggers)

The block form above scopes tags to the fiber. Sometimes it is more convenient to bind tags to a
single logger instance, for example when the logger belongs to an object with its own identity (an
ActiveRecord model or a background job).

Calling `tagged` (or its alias `with_tags`) **without a block** returns a new "child" logger that
permanently carries the supplied tags. Every entry from that child, and only that child, includes
them, even across threads:

~~~ruby
class Cart
  include SemanticLogger::Loggable

  def initialize(id)
    @id     = id
    # Bind this Cart's identity to its own logger instance.
    @logger = SemanticLogger["Cart"].tagged(cart_id: id)
  end

  attr_reader :logger

  def add_item(item_id)
    # Automatically tagged with cart_id, without wrapping every method in a block.
    logger.info("Added item", item_id: item_id)
  end
end
~~~

Positional and named tags can be mixed:

~~~ruby
logger = SemanticLogger["Payments"].tagged("billing", region: "eu")
logger.info("Charged card") # tagged with ["billing"] and {region: "eu"}
~~~

Notes:

- The original logger is never modified; `tagged` returns a copy. Child loggers can be nested, each
  level adding to the tags inherited from its parent.
- Instance tags combine with any thread tags from a surrounding `tagged` block: positional thread tags
  come first, then the logger's instance tags. For named tags, the logger's own tags win on a key
  conflict, since they represent its identity.
- Child loggers are ordinary instances, registered nowhere, so they are garbage collected along with
  the object that owns them.

## Going further

The features above cover everyday logging. The rest of this guide covers less common needs.

### Name your threads

Semantic Logger includes the thread name in every entry. A thread that has no name is identified by
its object id instead:

~~~
2013-11-07 16:25:14.279 I [35841:16] (0.0ms) ExternalSupplier -- Calling external interface
~~~

Give a thread a readable name so it stands out in the logs:

~~~ruby
Thread.current.name = "User calculation thread 32"
~~~

~~~
2013-11-07 16:26:02.744 I [35841:User calculation thread 32] (0.0ms) ExternalSupplier -- Calling external interface
~~~

Keep the name unique, otherwise concurrent threads are hard to tell apart. For example, number the
threads in a pool:

~~~ruby
workers = Array.new(5) do |i|
  Thread.new do
    Thread.current.name = "calc #{i + 1}"
    # ...
  end
end
~~~

This is Ruby's own `Thread#name=`, so the name must be a String, and Ruby raises for one that
contains a NUL byte or is not in an ASCII-compatible encoding. Ruby also gives the name to the
operating system, so it shows up in tools that list threads, such as `top -H`, debuggers, and
profilers. Log entries show the whole name, but Linux keeps only its first 15 bytes, so keep the
name short, or put the part that tells threads apart first. Semantic Logger keeps its own thread
names short for the same reason, naming each after its appender, such as `SL Appenders` and
`SL File`.

On JRuby, naming a thread also names the underlying JVM thread, which shows up when monitoring the
JVM with tools such as jconsole or jstack. JRuby names the main thread `main`, and a thread created
by Java code, such as a servlet container's request thread, is logged with its JVM thread name.

### Log from Ractors (experimental)

On Ruby 4.0 and later, code running in a [Ractor](https://docs.ruby-lang.org/en/4.0/Ractor.html)
logs as usual, and the entries are written by the appenders added in the main Ractor. Like Ruby's
own Ractor API, this is experimental, and may change in a minor release.

~~~ruby
SemanticLogger.add_appender(io: $stdout, formatter: :color)

context = SemanticLogger.tagged(job_id: 42) { SemanticLogger.context }
worker  = Ractor.new(context, name: "worker") do |job_context|
  SemanticLogger.with_context(job_context) do
    logger = SemanticLogger["Importer"]
    logger.info("Importing", rows: 1_000) # carries job_id: 42
  end
end
worker.join
~~~

Each entry is sent to the main Ractor, where a thread hands it to the appenders, so a Ractor never
waits on an appender. The thread name of an entry starts with the Ractor's name, or its number, as in
`worker/12345` or `ractor-3/12345`.

Things to know:

- A new Ractor does not have the tags of the code that created it. Hand them over with
  [`SemanticLogger.context`](#hand-tags-to-another-thread-or-fiber), as shown above.
- Add appenders, and change any setting, such as `SemanticLogger.default_level`, in the main Ractor.
  Doing so in another Ractor raises `Ractor::IsolationError`.
- Each Ractor has its own loggers: a `Loggable` class has a logger of its own in each Ractor, and so
  does a class with `SemanticLogger.cache_loggers` enabled. Setting a level on the main Ractor's logger
  therefore does not change the level of a Ractor's logger; the global default level applies to both.
- `on_log` subscribers run for an entry logged in a Ractor only when they are shareable, such as a
  module with a `call` method, or a block made with `Ractor.shareable_proc`.
- An entry is copied to the main Ractor. A value that Ruby cannot copy, such as a Proc in the payload,
  is written as its `inspect`, and so is such a value held by a logged exception. The extra detail
  that Ruby adds to some exceptions' messages, such as did_you_mean's "Did you mean?" suggestions, is
  not written for an exception logged in a Ractor.
- `SemanticLogger.flush` in a Ractor waits until the main Ractor has written that Ractor's entries.
- The main Ractor accepts entries from other Ractors as fast as they are logged, so logging never
  slows a Ractor down, however busy the appenders are. `max_queue_size` and `non_blocking` then apply
  to the entries as usual, once the receiving thread hands them to the processor. In sync mode, too,
  the receiving thread writes them.
- On Ruby 3.4 and earlier, logging from a Ractor other than the main one raises
  `Ractor::IsolationError`, as it always has.

### Change one class's level at runtime

Because each class has its own logger, you can change one class's level on the fly, for example to
temporarily turn on `:trace` while diagnosing an issue, without touching the rest of the application:

~~~ruby
# Raise the detail for this one class
ExternalSupplier.logger.level = :trace

# ... reproduce the issue; trace entries from ExternalSupplier are now logged ...

# Return it to following the global default level
ExternalSupplier.logger.level = nil
~~~

To change the global default level for every logger that has not been set explicitly, set
`SemanticLogger.default_level`. See [Configuration](config.html#default-log-level), and
[Signals](operations.html#linux-signals) for changing it in a running process without a restart.

### Silence noisy code

`silence` raises the level within a block, on the current fiber only, to quiet a noisy section:

~~~ruby
# Within this block, log only :error and above
logger.silence do
  logger.info "not logged"
  logger.warn "not logged"
  logger.error "but errors are logged"
end
~~~

It can also lower the level within the block, to get more detail from one section:

~~~ruby
logger.silence(:trace) do
  logger.debug "logged, even though the default level is higher"
end
~~~

`silence` has no effect on loggers whose level was set explicitly (those that do not follow the global
default), and does not affect threads or fibers started inside the block, unless they are handed the
block's [context](#hand-tags-to-another-thread-or-fiber).

### Map a noisy gem's debug logs to trace

Some third party gems log a lot at `:debug`, because they do not have Semantic Logger's `:trace`
level. Wrap such a library's logger in `SemanticLogger::DebugAsTraceLogger` so its `debug` calls are
recorded as `:trace`, keeping them out of your `:debug` output:

~~~ruby
logger = SemanticLogger::DebugAsTraceLogger.new("NoisyLibrary")
logger.debug "Some very low level noisy message" # logged as :trace
~~~

### Capture causal (nested) exceptions

When one exception is rescued and another raised, Ruby records the original as the new exception's
`cause`. Semantic Logger logs the whole chain automatically:

~~~ruby
def oh_no
  File.new("filename", "w").read # raises IOError: not opened for reading
rescue IOError
  raise RuntimeError, "Failed to write to file"
end

begin
  oh_no
rescue StandardError => exception
  logger.error("Failed calling oh_no", exception)
end
~~~

Both exceptions are logged, the second backtrace starting at `Cause:`:

~~~
E [17641:70311685126260 demo.rb:17] Demo -- Failed calling oh_no -- Exception: RuntimeError: Failed to write to file
demo.rb:6:in `rescue in oh_no'
demo.rb:2:in `oh_no'
Cause: IOError: not opened for reading
demo.rb:4:in `read'
demo.rb:4:in `oh_no'
~~~

### Replace the logger in other gems

Rails Semantic Logger already replaces the loggers for many gems. When using Semantic Logger
stand-alone, hand them a Semantic Logger instance yourself:

~~~ruby
Resque.logger  = SemanticLogger[Resque]  if defined?(Resque) && Resque.respond_to?(:logger)
Mongoid.logger = SemanticLogger[Mongoid] if defined?(Mongoid)

Sidekiq.configure_server do |config|
  config.logger = SemanticLogger[Sidekiq]
end
~~~

## Next steps

- [Log Event](log.html): the structure of every entry your filters, formatters, and appenders
  receive.
- [Configuration](config.html): global settings, custom formatters, filtering, and destinations.
- [Operations](operations.html): process forking, performance tuning, signals, and log rotation.

<!-- source: docs/config.md -->

## Configuration

Semantic Logger is configured once, when your application starts, by setting a few global values
and adding one or more appenders (destinations). This page walks through that configuration from
the simplest, most common settings at the top to formatter and appender customization further down.

Production concerns such as process forking, performance tuning, signals, and log rotation are
covered separately in [Operations](operations.html).

If you are using Rails, most of this is handled for you by the companion gem
[rails_semantic_logger](rails.html); configure it through `config.semantic_logger` and
`config.rails_semantic_logger` instead.

A minimal configuration looks like this:

~~~ruby
require "semantic_logger"

# 1. Choose the lowest level to log.
SemanticLogger.default_level = :info

# 2. Add at least one destination.
SemanticLogger.add_appender(io: $stdout, formatter: :color)

# 3. Get a logger and use it.
logger = SemanticLogger["MyApp"]
logger.info("Ready")
~~~

The sections below explain each piece, and everything you can tune around it.

---

## Global settings

These module level settings apply to the whole process. Set them once, before or just after adding
your appenders.

### Default log level

Semantic Logger logs `:info` and above by default. The levels, from most detail to least, are:

    :trace, :debug, :info, :warn, :error, :fatal

Setting the level to `:debug` includes `:info`, `:warn`, `:error`, and `:fatal`, but not `:trace`.
To log everything, set the global default to `:trace`:

~~~ruby
SemanticLogger.default_level = :trace
~~~

Every logger uses this global default unless it has been given its own level. Once a logger has an
explicit level, changing `SemanticLogger.default_level` no longer affects it. An appender does not
use the global default: without a level of its own it writes every entry that the loggers emit, and
with one it keeps only those at or above it (see [Per-appender settings](#per-appender-settings)).
The global default can also be changed at runtime (see [Signals](operations.html#linux-signals) for
changing it in a running process without a restart):

~~~ruby
SemanticLogger.default_level = :debug
~~~

### Application, environment, and host name

Semantic Logger can include the application name, environment, and host name in every log entry.
Not every appender uses these fields, but structured appenders (JSON, Elasticsearch, Splunk, and so
on) and centralized logging systems rely on them to tell apart logs coming from different
applications and servers:

~~~ruby
SemanticLogger.application = "my_app"
SemanticLogger.environment = "production"
SemanticLogger.host        = "web-server-1"
~~~

When not set explicitly, these default to:

- `application`: the `SEMANTIC_LOGGER_APP` environment variable, otherwise `"Semantic Logger"`.
- `environment`: the first of `SEMANTIC_LOGGER_ENV`, `RAILS_ENV`, or `RACK_ENV` that is set.
- `host`: the machine's host name.

Each value can also be overridden for a single appender by passing `application:`, `environment:`,
or `host:` to `add_appender` (see [Per-appender settings](#per-appender-settings)).

The default and `:color` text formatters do not print these values. To see them in text output, use
the `:pattern` formatter with `%{application}`, `%{environment}`, or `%{host}`, or a structured
formatter such as `:json`.

### Capturing backtraces

Semantic Logger can capture the backtrace of the code that created each log entry, include its file
name and line number in the output, and forward it to error services such as Bugsnag. To record only
where each entry was logged, at a fraction of the cost, see
[Recording where each entry was logged](#recording-where-each-entry-was-logged) below.

Capturing a backtrace is expensive, so it is controlled by its own level, which defaults to
`:error`. Only entries at this level or higher capture a backtrace:

~~~ruby
# Capture backtraces for :error and :fatal entries (the default)
SemanticLogger.backtrace_level = :error
~~~

To capture a backtrace for every entry, set it to `:trace`. To turn backtrace capture off entirely,
set it to `nil`. It is strongly recommended to leave this at `:error` or higher in production.

### Recording where each entry was logged

To record the file, line, and method of the code that made each log call, set `call_site_level`.
Entries at this level or higher record their call site. It is off (`nil`) by default:

~~~ruby
# Record where :info and higher entries were logged
SemanticLogger.call_site_level = :info

# Every entry
SemanticLogger.call_site_level = :trace

# Off (the default)
SemanticLogger.call_site_level = nil
~~~

In Rails, set it in `config/application.rb` with `config.semantic_logger.call_site_level = :info`.

The text formatters then show the method after the file name and line number, and the JSON formatter
adds a `method` field:

~~~
2026-11-15 13:58:05.906754 I [8462:main order.rb:42 Order#submit] Order -- Submitted
~~~

~~~json
{"file":"/app/models/order.rb","line":42,"method":"Order#submit","name":"Order","message":"Submitted"}
~~~

Unlike a backtrace, the call site is found by reading only the stack frames up to the code that made
the log call. A backtrace builds a String for every frame of the stack, so its cost grows with the
depth of the stack:

| | `backtrace_level` | `call_site_level` |
|-|-------------------|-------------------|
| Records | The whole stack, as an Array of Strings | The file, line, and method of the log call |
| Time added to a `logger.info` call, 100 frames deep | About 16 µs (Ruby 3.2) to 26 µs (Ruby 4.0) | About 1.5 µs |
| On a deeper stack | Grows with the depth | The same |
| Default | `:error` | `nil` (off) |

(Measured on an Apple M5; a `logger.info` call without either takes about 1.3 µs. Reading the stack
costs much more on JRuby: about 25 µs for the call site, and 180 µs for a backtrace.) The call site is
cheap enough to record for every entry in most applications, but it still about doubles the time a
log call spends on the thread that logs, so measure it when an application logs at a very high rate.

The method is the label Ruby gives the frame in a backtrace:

| Code that logged | Ruby 3.4 and later | Ruby 3.2, 3.3, and JRuby |
|------------------|--------------------|--------------------------|
| Instance method | `Order#submit` | `submit` |
| Class method | `Order.find_open` | `find_open` |
| Block inside a method | `block in Order#submit` | `block in submit` |
| Method defined with `define_method` | `block in <class:Order>` | `block in <class:Order>` |
| Outside any method | `<main>`, `<class:Order>` | `<main>`, `<class:Order>` |

JRuby gives a method defined with `define_method` its name, such as `submit`.

Where each formatter writes the call site:

| Formatter | File and line | Method |
|-----------|---------------|--------|
| `:default`, `:color`, `:one_line`, `:syslog` | `order.rb:42`, after the thread name | After the line number |
| `:pattern` | `%{file_name}`, `%{line}` | `%{method}` |
| `:json`, `:raw`, `:syslog_cee`, `:fluentd` (with `need_process_info: true`), and the appenders that use them | `file`, `line` | `method` |
| `:ecs` | `log.origin.file.name`, `log.origin.file.line` | `log.origin.function` |
| `:new_relic_logs` | `file.name`, `line.number` | `method.name` |
| `:open_telemetry` | `code.file.path`, `code.line.number` | `code.function.name` |

The `:logfmt` and `:loki` formatters write neither. A custom formatter reads the call site from
[`log.call_site`](log.html#attributes).

Which code counts as the call site:

* When the log call, or a `measure_*` call, supplies `call_site:`, that call site. Code that logs on
  behalf of other code, such as a log subscriber, can say which code the entry is about with a
  `Thread::Backtrace::Location` (for example from `Thread.each_caller_location`) or a
  `SemanticLogger::CallSite`, or that it has no such code with `false`, which records no call site
  without reading the stack for one. `nil` means none was supplied, so the call site is found as
  usual. A supplied call site is only recorded when the entry is at or above `call_site_level`, so
  that it never adds a call site to the output of an application that has not turned call sites on:

  ~~~ruby
  # The application code that ran the query, or none when no frame is the application's
  logger.debug(message: "Order Load", duration: 0.4,
               call_site: backtrace_cleaner.first_clean_location || false)
  logger.info(message: "Started GET /orders", call_site: false)
  ~~~

  A String, or any other value that parsed data can hold, is not accepted as a call site, nor is a
  `CallSite` without a String path, an Integer line, and a String or `nil` label: a log call logs it
  as part of the payload, and a `measure_*` call ignores it. An entry
  with `call_site: false` that captures a backtrace (see `backtrace_level`), or logs an exception,
  still has a file name and line number from that backtrace, as the last point below says.
* The first frame outside Semantic Logger, `rails_semantic_logger`, and Ruby's internal files (paths
  that start with `<internal:`). So an entry logged by a `measure_*` call, or by a logging block,
  records the code that called the logger. When the logger is called through `public_send`,
  `Method#call`, or `UnboundMethod#bind_call`, the call site is the code that called that method. (On
  JRuby, `Method#call` inside a block records the right file and line, but the label `block in call`.)
  Code in Ruby's standard library that calls the logger for you, such as a method that `Forwardable`
  delegates, is recorded as the call site: add its path to `call_site_skip_paths` (see below).
* When the log call supplies a `backtrace:`, the first line of that backtrace. For example
  `logger.backtrace` passes the backtrace of the thread it logs, and `rails_semantic_logger` passes
  the application code that ran a SQL query when it captures a backtrace for the entry (see
  `backtrace_level` above). A backtrace returned by a logging block does not change the call site.
* Entries that `rails_semantic_logger` logs for Rails' own events, such as `Processing`,
  `Completed`, `Rendered`, and SQL entries without a backtrace, are logged from Active Support's
  notifications, so their call site is an Active Support frame rather than the application's code.
* With a call site, an entry's file name and line number are the call site's, also for an entry that
  logs an exception. Without one, they still come from a captured backtrace, or else the first line
  of the exception's backtrace.

Code that logs on behalf of its caller, such as an application's own logging helper, would always be
recorded as the call site. Skip its frames with `call_site_skip_paths`, so that entries record the
code that called it. Each entry matches any file whose path includes it:

~~~ruby
# AuditLog.record(...) logs for its callers
SemanticLogger.call_site_skip_paths = ["app/lib/audit_log.rb"]

# Every file of a gem that wraps the logger
SemanticLogger.call_site_skip_paths = ["app/lib/audit_log.rb", "/my_logging_gem/"]
~~~

### Cleaning backtraces

Most of an exception's backtrace is usually gems and Ruby itself, with the application's own frames
somewhere in the middle. A backtrace cleaner leaves out or shortens lines before they are logged.
Set the application's cleaner once:

~~~ruby
SemanticLogger.backtrace_cleaner = Rails.backtrace_cleaner
~~~

A cleaner is any object that responds to `#clean`, as `ActiveSupport::BacktraceCleaner` does, or to
`#call`, such as a Proc. It is given each backtrace as an Array of Strings, and returns the lines to
log:

~~~ruby
app_root = "#{Dir.pwd}/"
SemanticLogger.backtrace_cleaner = lambda do |lines|
  lines.select { |line| line.start_with?(app_root) }.map { |line| line.delete_prefix(app_root) }
end
~~~

Only the text and JSON output changes: the `:default`, `:color`, `:pattern`, `:one_line`
(which does not write backtraces), `:syslog`, `:json`, and `:fluentd` formatters clean the backtrace
of the logged exception and of each exception that caused it. So do the appenders that use `:json`
unless given another formatter: `:http`, `:elasticsearch_http`, `:tcp`, `:udp`, `:kafka`,
`:rabbitmq`, and `:cloudwatch_logs`. To send full backtraces to a log service through one of them,
give it `formatter: {json: {backtrace_cleaner: false}}`.

The exception itself is never changed, so appenders that send the exception to an error service,
such as Sentry, Bugsnag, or Honeybadger, still send its full backtrace. The other formatters,
including `:raw` and the formatters written for a particular service, such as `:ecs`, `:loki`,
`:new_relic_logs`, and `:open_telemetry`, write the full backtrace. So do the `:elasticsearch`,
`:opensearch`, `:mongodb`, `:graylog`, `:splunk_http`, and `:honeybadger_insights` appenders, which
build their entries with formatters of their own: giving one of them a `formatter` replaces how it
builds its entries.

The `backtrace_cleaner` option of an appender's formatter chooses for that appender:

| Value | Cleans backtraces with |
|-------|------------------------|
| `true` | The application's cleaner, `SemanticLogger.backtrace_cleaner`, when one is set. The default for the formatters listed above. |
| `false` | Nothing: the full backtrace is written. The default for every other formatter. |
| A cleaner | That cleaner, in place of the application's. |

~~~ruby
# Keep full backtraces in the JSON file:
SemanticLogger.add_appender(file_name: "production.json", formatter: {json: {backtrace_cleaner: false}})

# Clean the backtraces in logfmt output too:
SemanticLogger.add_appender(io: $stdout, formatter: {logfmt: {backtrace_cleaner: true}})

# Use a cleaner of its own for one appender:
SemanticLogger.add_appender(io: $stdout, formatter: {color: {backtrace_cleaner: MyCleaner.new}})
~~~

Notes:

* When the cleaner leaves out every line, for example for an exception raised entirely inside gems,
  the full backtrace is logged, so the only clue to where it came from is never lost. The full
  backtrace is also logged when the cleaner does not return an Array, or raises an error, which is
  reported to the internal logger.
* The cleaner is called on the appenders' threads, not the thread that logged the entry, so it must be
  thread safe. Its result is kept with the entry, so it is normally called once for each exception,
  however many appenders write it. Appenders that write the same entry at the same moment can each
  call it.
* The application's cleaner is looked up as each entry is written, so it can be set before or after
  the appenders are added.
* The file name and line number of an entry are not cleaned. They are where the entry was logged when
  it has a call site (see `call_site_level` above) or captured a backtrace (see `backtrace_level`
  above), and otherwise the first line of the exception's backtrace.

### Redacting sensitive keys

Name the keys whose values must never be logged, such as passwords and access tokens, and their
values are replaced with `[FILTERED]` in the payload, named tags, context, and metric dimensions of
every log entry, at any depth, before any appender writes it:

~~~ruby
SemanticLogger.sensitive_keys = %i[passw secret token _key authorization cookie]
~~~

Symbols and Strings match any key whose name contains them, ignoring case, as in Rails'
`config.filter_parameters`, and an `ActiveSupport::ParameterFilter`, a Regexp, or a Proc can be given
instead. rails_semantic_logger sets it from `config.filter_parameters`. See
[Redacting sensitive data](security.html#redacting-sensitive-data) for what is matched and redacted,
and what is not.

### Caching loggers

By default `SemanticLogger[...]` returns a brand new logger instance on every call. Enable logger
caching to have a single shared logger returned per class:

~~~ruby
SemanticLogger.cache_loggers = true

SemanticLogger[MyClass].equal?(SemanticLogger[MyClass]) # => true
~~~

This makes it possible to obtain a logger once and later change its level (or filter) so that every
holder of that logger sees the change:

~~~ruby
SemanticLogger[MyClass].level = :debug
~~~

Notes:

- Caching is opt-in and disabled by default.
- Only Classes and Modules are cached. A String always returns a new instance, since string call
  sites commonly want an independent logger (for example to set a different level per call site).
- Anonymous classes (those without a name) are never cached.
- With caching enabled, `SemanticLogger[MyClass]` and the `SemanticLogger::Loggable` mixin's
  `MyClass.logger` return the same instance.
- Setting `SemanticLogger.cache_loggers = false` clears the cache. It can also be cleared explicitly
  with `SemanticLogger.clear_logger_cache`, for example after redefining a class.

---

## Per-appender settings

Each destination is added with `SemanticLogger.add_appender`. The full catalogue of destinations,
and the options specific to each, is in [Appenders](appenders.html). Each call adds one destination,
given as one of `file_name:`, `io:`, `logger:`, `appender:`, or `metric:`; to write to several, call
it once for each. Given more than one of them, `add_appender` raises an `ArgumentError` that names
them. A destination given as `nil` is not one, so that
settings of which only one is set can be passed on, such as
`file_name: options[:log_file], io: options[:log_io]`.

In addition to its own settings, almost every appender accepts these common options:

| Option | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| `level` | Only write entries at this level or higher to this appender. Without it, an appender writes every entry it receives; those that send errors to a service, such as Bugsnag and Sentry, default to `:error` instead, and Honeybadger Insights to `:info`. Each logger only emits entries at or above its own level, which defaults to `SemanticLogger.default_level`, so set an appender's `level` to keep fewer entries than the loggers emit. |
| `formatter` | How to format the output, for example `:default`, `:color`, or `:json`. A [block given to `add_appender`](#formatter-as-a-block-or-proc) takes its place. See [Custom formatters](#custom-formatters). |
| `filter` | A `Regexp` or `Proc` selecting which entries this appender accepts. See [Filtering](#filtering). |
| `application`, `environment`, `host` | Override the global values for this appender only. |

A per-appender `level` lets each destination keep a different subset of the logs. For example, keep
a full trace log and a separate warnings-only log. An appender only receives the entries that the
loggers emit, so for the trace log to receive trace entries the loggers must emit them too:

~~~ruby
require "semantic_logger"

# Loggers emit every entry:
SemanticLogger.default_level = :trace

# Everything at :trace and above:
SemanticLogger.add_appender(file_name: "log/trace.log",    level: :trace)

# Only warnings and above:
SemanticLogger.add_appender(file_name: "log/warnings.log", level: :warn)
~~~

---

## Filtering

A filter decides, for each log entry, whether it should be written. Use a filter to:

* Quiet a noisy library without modifying its code.
* Send only certain messages to a particular destination (for example, a dedicated audit file).
* Strip sensitive data out of a message before it is written.

### A filter is one of three things

1. **A regular expression.** It is matched against the **class name** of the logger (the value you
   passed to `SemanticLogger["..."]`). The entry is kept only if the class name matches.

   ```ruby
   filter: /MyClass/
   ```

2. **A Proc (or lambda).** It receives the whole log event and must return `true` to **keep** the
   entry. Returning anything else (`false`, `nil`, a string, ...) **drops** it.

   ```ruby
   filter: ->(log) { log.message !~ /heartbeat/ }
   ```

3. **A module or object that responds to `.call`.** Same contract as a Proc, but in a named,
   reusable, testable place. Reach for this when the logic grows beyond a one-liner.

   ```ruby
   module ExcludeHealthChecks
     def self.call(log)
       !log.message.to_s.start_with?("GET /health")
     end
   end

   filter: ExcludeHealthChecks
   ```

> **The most common gotcha:** a Proc or `.call` filter must return **exactly `true`** to keep an
> entry. `0`, `"yes"`, or any truthy-but-not-`true` value will silently drop the entry. When in
> doubt, end the filter with an explicit boolean expression.

The log event passed to a Proc or module filter carries every attribute of the message: `name`,
`message`, `level`, `payload`, `tags`, `named_tags`, `duration`, `exception`, and more. The full
list is in [Log Event](log.html).

### Where a filter can be attached

* **On an appender** (a destination). The filter affects only what *that one destination* writes.
  Use this to give one file or service a curated subset of the logs.
* **On a logger instance.** The filter affects *every* appender, but only for entries coming
  *through that one logger*. Use this to quiet a single class or library across all destinations.

### Example: appender filter with a regular expression

Keep a full log in `development.log`, and additionally maintain a `my_class.log` that contains
**only** the messages from `MyClass`:

```ruby
require "semantic_logger"

# Step 1: a catch-all appender that records everything.
SemanticLogger.add_appender(file_name: "development.log")

# Step 2: a second appender that only keeps entries whose logger class name matches /MyClass/.
SemanticLogger.add_appender(file_name: "my_class.log", filter: /MyClass/)

# Step 3: log from two different classes.
SemanticLogger["MyClass"].info "Written to BOTH development.log and my_class.log"
SemanticLogger["OtherClass"].info "Written ONLY to development.log"
```

You can also set the filter after the appender exists:

```ruby
appender        = SemanticLogger.add_appender(file_name: "my_class.log")
appender.filter = /MyClass/
```

### Example: appender filter with a Proc

A `summary.log` that contains everything **except** the (very chatty) messages from `MyClass`:

```ruby
SemanticLogger.add_appender(
  file_name: "summary.log",
  # Keep the entry (return true) unless it came from MyClass.
  filter: ->(log) { log.name != "MyClass" }
)
```

Because the Proc receives the whole log event, you can filter on anything:

```ruby
# Drop entries below a duration threshold (only keep slow measure calls).
filter: ->(log) { log.duration.to_f >= 100 }

# Drop a specific noisy message regardless of which class logged it.
filter: ->(log) { log.message !~ /\Aheartbeat/ }
```

### Example: rewriting a message inside a filter

A filter can also **modify** the log event before it is written, as long as it still returns `true`
so the (now edited) entry is kept. This is handy for removing sensitive data from a message in a
logger's filter, as below, or in `on_log`. To redact the values of sensitive keys in every entry, use
[`SemanticLogger.sensitive_keys`](#redacting-sensitive-keys) instead. Do not redact in an appender's
filter: every appender writes the same log event, so the appenders added before it have already
written the data. Resque, for example, logs the entire job payload,
which may contain private information:

```ruby
Resque.logger.filter = ->(log) do
  if log.name == "Resque" && (match = log.message.to_s.match(/\A(got|done): /))
    log.message = match[1] # replace the full payload with just the action
  end
  true # always return true so the (edited) message is still logged
end
```

### Example: logger filter to quiet a library

When a library lets you replace its logger, attach a filter to a logger instance to suppress its
noise everywhere it is logged, without touching any appender:

```ruby
logger        = SemanticLogger[Resque]
logger.filter = ->(log) { log.message !~ /\A\*\*\* Checking/ }
Resque.logger = logger
```

---

## Custom formatters

The formatter turns each log event into the text or JSON that an appender writes. Pass a
`formatter:` when adding an appender. The simplest options are the built-in formatters selected by
name (`:default`, `:color`, `:json`, `:logfmt`, and others; see [Appenders](appenders.html)). For
anything beyond those, you have three choices, in increasing order of effort: a pattern string, a
block or Proc, or a formatter class.

### Pattern formatter

For simple layout changes there is no need to write any code. The built-in `:pattern` formatter
builds each log line from a pattern string. Placeholders use the form `%{directive}`; to emit a
literal `%{...}`, escape it as `%%{...}`.

~~~ruby
# A message-only format on stdout, for end users:
SemanticLogger.add_appender(
  io:        $stdout,
  formatter: {pattern: {pattern: "%{message}"}}
)

# A timestamped format to a file:
SemanticLogger.add_appender(
  file_name: "application.log",
  formatter: {pattern: {pattern: "%{time} %{level} %{name} -- %{message}"}}
)
~~~

The pattern is parsed once when the appender is created, so formatting every entry is fast. An
unknown directive (or an argument supplied to a directive that does not take one) raises an error
immediately, when the appender is configured.

Available directives:

| Directive              | Description                                              |
|------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------|
| `%{time}`              | Formatted timestamp. A strftime format may be supplied, e.g. `%{time:%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S.%6N}`. |
| `%{level}`             | Full level name, e.g. `debug`.                           |
| `%{level_short}`       | Single character level, e.g. `D`.                        |
| `%{name}`              | Logger / class name.                                     |
| `%{message}`           | Log message.                                             |
| `%{payload}`           | Payload rendered as a string.                            |
| `%{exception_class}`   | Class of the logged exception, e.g. `RuntimeError`.      |
| `%{exception_message}` | Message of the logged exception.                         |
| `%{exception_details}` | Detail Ruby adds to the exception's message, such as did_you_mean suggestions. See [Exception details](#exception-details). |
| `%{backtrace}`         | Backtrace of the logged exception.                       |
| `%{duration}`          | Human readable duration, e.g. `1.2ms`.                   |
| `%{duration_ms}`       | Duration in milliseconds (numeric).                      |
| `%{thread_name}`       | Name of the thread that logged the message.              |
| `%{pid}`               | Process id.                                              |
| `%{file_name}`         | Ruby file name that logged the message, e.g. `app.rb`.   |
| `%{line}`              | Line number within the Ruby file, e.g. `42`.             |
| `%{method}`            | Method that logged the message, e.g. `Order#submit`, when the entry has a call site. See [Recording where each entry was logged](#recording-where-each-entry-was-logged). |
| `%{tags}`              | Tags, comma separated.                                   |
| `%{named_tags}`        | All named tags. One tag with `%{named_tags:request_id}`. |
| `%{host}`              | Host name.                                               |
| `%{application}`       | Application name.                                        |
| `%{environment}`       | Environment name.                                        |

When the pattern is omitted it defaults to a layout similar to the default text formatter:
`%{time} %{level} [%{pid}:%{thread_name}] %{name} -- %{message}`.

#### Example: a custom timestamp format

The `%{time}` directive accepts a [strftime](https://ruby-doc.org/core/Time.html#method-i-strftime)
format string, applied directly to the log time:

~~~ruby
SemanticLogger.add_appender(
  io:        $stdout,
  formatter: {pattern: {pattern: "%{time:%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S.%6N%z} %{level} -- %{message}"}}
)
# => 2017-04-05T01:05:52.868286+0000 info -- Hello World
~~~

#### Example: include a request id from the named tags

Named tags (set with `SemanticLogger.tagged(request_id: "...")`) can be pulled out individually with
`%{named_tags:key}`:

~~~ruby
SemanticLogger.add_appender(
  io:        $stdout,
  formatter: {pattern: {pattern: "%{time} %{level} [%{named_tags:request_id}] %{name} -- %{message}"}}
)
~~~

### Formatter as a block or Proc

For full control with minimal ceremony, give `add_appender` a block. It formats every entry written
to that appender. It is called with two arguments, the log event and the appender. A block, or a
Proc made with `proc`, may take just the log event; a lambda or method, passed with `&` or as
`formatter:`, must accept both arguments. For the structure of the log event, see
[Log Event](log.html). The appender holds the `host`, `application`, and `environment` to write
with the entry.

~~~ruby
SemanticLogger.application = "MyApp"

SemanticLogger.add_appender(io: $stdout) do |log, appender|
  "#{log.level.upcase} #{appender.application} #{log.name} -- #{log.message}"
end
# => INFO MyApp Order -- Order submitted
~~~

The block returns what the appender writes. For `io:`, `file_name:`, and `logger:`, return the entry
as a String: `io:` and `file_name:` write it followed by a newline, and `logger:` passes it to the
wrapped logger.

A block works the same way for an appender named by a Symbol. It takes the
place of the formatter the appender uses by default, so it returns what that formatter returns: a
String for the text and JSON destinations, such as `:tcp`, `:udp`, `:http`, and `:syslog` with its
default local url, and a Hash for those that store a document, such as `:elasticsearch` and
`:mongodb`. For `:loki`, and for `:syslog` with a `tcp://` or `udp://` url, the default formatter
builds the whole request body or syslog packet, so a block would have to build it too: use a
formatter class instead, such as a subclass of `SemanticLogger::Formatters::Loki` or
`SemanticLogger::Formatters::Syslog` (see [Formatter as a class](#formatter-as-a-class)). A metric
appender, such as `metric: :statsd` or `metric: :signalfx`, takes no log entries, so it takes no
formatter: a block, or `formatter:`, given to one raises an `ArgumentError` (see
[Metrics](metrics.html#add-a-metric-appender)).

~~~ruby
SemanticLogger.add_appender(file_name: "development.log") { |log| "#{log.name} -- #{log.message}" }
SemanticLogger.add_appender(appender: :tcp, server: "localhost:514") { |log| "#{log.level} #{log.message}" }
~~~

A block formats one entry at a time, so it cannot format the single request that `:http` and
`:loki` send for a whole batch when added with `batch: true`: those need a formatter
that implements `#batch(logs, logger)`, such as the one each uses by default. `add_appender` raises
an `ArgumentError` for a block, or any other formatter that cannot format a batch, given to one of
them with `batch: true`. Add it without `batch: true` to send one request for each entry, formatted
by the block.

When both a block and `formatter:` are given, the block takes precedence, and `formatter:` is
ignored.

The same formatter can be given to `formatter:` as a Proc, for example to share it between
appenders:

~~~ruby
formatter = proc do |log|
  # This formatter just returns the log event as a string
  log.inspect
end
SemanticLogger.add_appender(io: $stdout, formatter: formatter)
SemanticLogger.add_appender(file_name: "development.log", formatter: formatter)
~~~

An appender created with `new` and added as `appender:` or `metric:` already has its formatter, so
`add_appender` raises an `ArgumentError` for a block given with it, as it does for `formatter:` and
the other appender options. Give the block, or `formatter:`, to `new` instead:

~~~ruby
appender = SemanticLogger::Appender::Tcp.new(server: "localhost:514") { |log| "#{log.level} #{log.message}" }
SemanticLogger.add_appender(appender: appender)
~~~

### Formatter as a class

When the formatting logic is substantial or reused, subclass one of the built-in formatters and
override just the methods you want to change.

Override the default text formatter to upper-case the level name:

~~~ruby
class MyFormatter < SemanticLogger::Formatters::Default
  # Return the complete log level name in uppercase
  def level
    log.level.upcase
  end
end

SemanticLogger.add_appender(file_name: "development.log", formatter: MyFormatter.new)
~~~

The colorized formatter can be customized the same way, keeping its color codes:

~~~ruby
class MyFormatter < SemanticLogger::Formatters::Color
  def level
    "#{color}#{log.level.upcase}#{color_map.clear}"
  end
end

SemanticLogger.add_appender(file_name: "development.log", formatter: MyFormatter.new)
~~~

A common request is to leave out the process id, for example when running a single process per
container (where the pid is always 1):

~~~ruby
class NoPidFormatter < SemanticLogger::Formatters::Default
  # Leave out the pid
  def pid
  end
end

SemanticLogger.add_appender(file_name: "development.log", formatter: NoPidFormatter.new)
~~~

See
[SemanticLogger::Formatters::Default](https://github.com/reidmorrison/semantic_logger/blob/main/lib/semantic_logger/formatters/default.rb)
and
[SemanticLogger::Formatters::Color](https://github.com/reidmorrison/semantic_logger/blob/main/lib/semantic_logger/formatters/color.rb)
for all the methods that can be overridden.

To replace the formatter on an appender that is already installed, for example in a Rails app:

~~~ruby
# Find the file appender and replace its formatter:
appender = SemanticLogger.appenders.find { |a| a.is_a?(SemanticLogger::Appender::File) }
appender.formatter = MyFormatter.new
~~~

### Escaping control characters

By design, the human readable text formatters (`:default` and `:color`) write log messages exactly
as supplied, including newlines and ANSI color codes. This is intentional and useful: multi-line
messages and colorized output make local logs easier to read.

When log messages can contain untrusted, attacker-controlled data (for example a user name, request
parameter, or `User-Agent` header), those same characters can be abused. A newline can forge an
additional, fake log entry ("log forging"), and an ANSI escape sequence can spoof or hide terminal
output when the log is viewed in a terminal.

Structured formatters such as `:json` are not affected, because JSON encoding always escapes control
characters. They are the recommended choice when forwarding logs that may contain untrusted data to
a centralized logging system.

For the text formatters, enable the `escape_control_chars` option to replace control characters in
untrusted log data (the logger name, thread name, message, payload, tags, named tags, the message,
details, and backtrace lines of the logged exception, and the message and backtrace lines of each
exception that caused it) with a printable, escaped form. For example a newline is written as `\n`
and the ANSI escape as `\e`. The Unicode characters that control how text is shown are escaped too,
in the `\uXXXX` form: the C1 control characters (U+0080 to U+009F), the line and paragraph
separators (U+2028, U+2029), at which editors and some log viewers start a new line, and the
bidirectional controls (U+202A to U+202E, U+2066 to U+2069), such as the right-to-left override that
can make logged text read backwards. The option is **disabled by default** to preserve the existing
human readable output:

```ruby
# Text appender that escapes control characters in untrusted data:
SemanticLogger.add_appender(file_name: "production.log", formatter: {default: {escape_control_chars: true}})

# Colorized appender, still escaping control characters in the logged data
# (the formatter's own color codes are preserved):
SemanticLogger.add_appender(io: $stdout, formatter: {color: {escape_control_chars: true}})
```

The option only escapes the control characters in the logged data; it does not touch the formatter's
own decoration, so the `:color` formatter keeps emitting its color codes. It does render the payload
without Amazing Print's colors, and on a single line, since the colors and line breaks Amazing Print
adds cannot be told apart from those in the data. The text formatters still lay out an exception and
its backtrace over several lines, since that layout is generated by Semantic Logger rather than
supplied as log data. The `:syslog` formatter, which escapes control characters by
default, is the exception: it also escapes the newlines between an exception and its backtrace lines,
so that each entry is a single line. The pattern formatter supports the same option (`{pattern:
{pattern: "...", escape_control_chars: true}}`), and the syslog, TCP, and UDP appenders enable it
where appropriate; see [Appenders](appenders.html).

### Exception details

Since Ruby 3.2, Ruby keeps some of the most useful information about an exception out of its
`message`, and adds it in `Exception#detailed_message` instead: did_you_mean suggestions, the
error_highlight snippet that points at the failing call, and any detail an exception class adds by
overriding `#detailed_message`. Semantic Logger logs that detail, without repeating the class name
that Ruby also adds, on the line after the exception message:

~~~
2026-10-25 12:00:00.000000 E [12345:1234 orders.rb:12] Orders -- Failed to ship -- Exception: NoMethodError: undefined method 'upcas' for an instance of String
Did you mean?  upcase
               upcase!
orders.rb:12:in 'Orders#ship'
...
~~~

The `log_exception_details` formatter option controls it:

| Value | Logs |
|-------|------|
| `true` | The detail, without the error_highlight source snippet. |
| `:with_source` | The detail, including the error_highlight source snippet. It is about 100 times slower, because error_highlight re-parses the source file of the failing line, and it copies source code into the log. |
| `false` | No detail. The exception message is unchanged either way. |

It defaults to `true` for the `:default`, `:color`, and `:pattern` formatters, and to `false` for
every other formatter, including `:one_line` and the syslog formatters, so their output does not
change. The syslog appender also turns it off for the formatter it uses with a local syslog daemon.
When enabled, `:one_line` joins the detail onto the same line, after ` -- `. With the `:json`
formatter and the others built on `:raw`, it adds an `exception.details` field (and `details`
within each `cause`), which `:logfmt` writes as `exception_details`:

```ruby
# Include the error_highlight source snippet in development:
SemanticLogger.add_appender(io: $stdout, formatter: {color: {log_exception_details: :with_source}})

# Add exception.details to JSON output:
SemanticLogger.add_appender(file_name: "production.json", formatter: {json: {log_exception_details: true}})
```

The pattern formatter's `%{exception_details}` directive interpolates the detail.

Notes:

* On Ruby 3.2, a `NameError` or `NoMethodError` calls `inspect` on its receiver every time its
  message is built, and logging the detail builds it twice more. If the receivers of logged
  exceptions are slow to inspect, set `log_exception_details: false`. Ruby 3.3 and later do not
  inspect the receiver.
* An exception class that overrides `#detailed_message` without accepting extra keyword arguments
  (`def detailed_message(highlight: false)`) cannot be asked to leave out error_highlight's source
  snippet. When error_highlight decorates that exception (a `NameError`, `TypeError`, or
  `ArgumentError`), its detail is only logged with `:with_source`.

---

## Custom appenders

To write your own log appender it should meet the following requirements:

* Inherit from `SemanticLogger::Subscriber`.
* In the initializer, connect to the resource being logged to.
* Implement `#log(log)`, which writes to the relevant resource.
* Implement `#flush` if the resource can be flushed.
* Write a test for the new appender.

The `#log` method receives the log event as its parameter. For its structure, see
[Log Event](log.html).

Basic outline for an appender:

~~~ruby
require "semantic_logger"

class SimpleAppender < SemanticLogger::Subscriber
  attr_reader :url

  # Add additional arguments to the initializer while supporting all existing ones.
  def initialize(url:, **args, &block)
    super(**args, &block)
    @url = url
  end

  # Display the log struct and the text formatted output
  def log(log)
    # Display the raw log structure
    p log

    # Display the formatted output
    puts format_log(log)
  end

  # Optional
  def flush
    puts "Flush :)"
  end

  # Optional
  def close
    puts "Closing :)"
  end
end
~~~

Do not give the appender an option of the same name as one that `super` already accepts, such as
`host` or `level`: the appender's own keyword would take the value, so `super` would never receive
it. Call `super` before setting the appender's own instance variables, since `super` sets those of
every appender, such as `@name` and `@host`.

When the appender runs asynchronously (`async: true` or batching), an exception raised by `#log`
discards the message, and the worker thread backs off before writing the next one, on the basis
that the destination may be briefly unavailable. An exception caused by the content of one message
says nothing about whether the destination is available, and nor does one that writing the
message again cannot fix, such as a request the destination refuses outright for its credentials,
so the thread carries on straight away instead. `#message_error?(exception)` decides which is
which, and these are the message errors. Format each message with `format_log(log)` (or
a batch with `format_batch(logs)`) rather than `formatter.call`: any error the
formatter raises, including a `ScriptError` such as `NotImplementedError`, which would otherwise
stop the worker thread, is then raised as a `SemanticLogger::Subscriber::FormatError`, which
`#message_error?` recognizes, since a formatter can only fail because of the content of the message.
By default it also recognizes the errors raised when serializing a value that cannot be written
(`JSON::GeneratorError`, `JSON::NestingError`, `EncodingError`, and `FloatDomainError`). Override it
to recognize errors your appender's client raises for content it cannot write:

~~~ruby
def message_error?(exception)
  exception.is_a?(MyClient::InvalidDocument) || super
end
~~~

Any other error is the destination's, and discards the message (or the batch) by default, since
the write may have stored some or all of it. When the write that raised it cannot have stored any of
the messages, and writing them again later may succeed, such as when the appender could not connect,
or the destination answered that it is unavailable for now, return `true` from
`#wrote_nothing?(exception)`. The worker thread then writes the same message, or batch, again once
it has backed off. Once the destination has answered it with a failure after it was written again 3
times, the worker thread discards it and carries on with the next one. Keep the default, `false`,
whenever the destination may have stored them, such as when its answer timed out, since writing
them again would store them twice, and when writing them again is bound to fail the same way. While
a flush or close is waiting, the message or batch is discarded either way, so that the flush does
not wait out the back-offs.

When the write never reached the destination, such as when the appender could not connect, also
return `true` from `#not_sent?(exception)`, which is asked only once `#wrote_nothing?` has returned
`true`. Writing it again after such a failure does not count towards the 3 times, since the
destination has said nothing about the message, so that an outage loses no messages until the
worker thread gives up after `async_max_retries`:

~~~ruby
def wrote_nothing?(exception)
  not_sent?(exception) || exception.is_a?(MyClient::ServiceUnavailable)
end

def not_sent?(exception)
  exception.is_a?(MyClient::ConnectionRefused)
end
~~~

When `#log` or `#batch` writes the messages in more than one request, return `false` for an error
from any request after the first: the destination stored the messages of the earlier ones, which
would otherwise be written again. That includes a subclass of `SemanticLogger::Appender::Http`
whose `#log` or `#batch` calls `post` more than once.

A `SystemStackError` is handled separately: the message is discarded, and since a thread must not
overflow its stack twice (on macOS that crashes Ruby), the worker carries on in a new thread. Do not
rescue it in `#log` or `#batch`.

An appender that supports batching implements `#batch(logs)`. When `#batch` raises a message error,
the whole batch is discarded by default, since it may already have written some of the messages.
If `#batch` writes nothing unless every message can be written, for example because it formats
them all into one request before sending it, return `true` from `#batch_all_or_nothing?`. The batch
is then split up and retried, so that only the offending message is discarded:

~~~ruby
def batch(logs)
  client.send_all(logs.map { |log| format_log(log) })
end

def batch_all_or_nothing?
  true
end
~~~

A message error that the destination raises for any batch, whatever messages it holds, such as a
request refused for its credentials or its url, would be raised again for every part. Recognize it in
`#message_error?`, since writing the batch again cannot fix it, and return `true` from
`#fails_any_batch?(exception)` for it, so that the whole batch is discarded at once, rather than
every message sent again on its own to be refused in turn. `#fails_any_batch?` is asked only about
a message error, and returns `false` by default:

~~~ruby
def message_error?(exception)
  exception.is_a?(MyClient::Unauthorized) || exception.is_a?(MyClient::InvalidDocument) || super
end

def fails_any_batch?(exception)
  exception.is_a?(MyClient::Unauthorized)
end
~~~

The HTTP appenders answer both from the status of the response: a request rejected with a `400`,
`413`, or `422` is a message error that only some of the messages cause, and one rejected with any
other 4xx but `408` and `429`, such as a `401`, `403`, or `404`, is one that fails any batch.

A destination that stores the messages of a batch in order, and stops at the first one it rejects,
may say which one that is. Return its position in the batch, counted from 0, from
`#rejected_entry(exception)`: the messages before it are then counted as written, it is discarded
(with every message after it, when `#fails_any_batch?` is true), and the messages after it are
written again as a batch, so that none is written twice. It returns `nil` by default, when the
appender cannot tell. The `:splunk_http` appender answers it from the HTTP Event Collector's
`invalid-event-number`:

~~~ruby
def rejected_entry(exception)
  exception.rejected_index if exception.is_a?(MyClient::Rejected)
end
~~~

`#batch_all_or_nothing?` says nothing about an error from the destination: a batch formatted before
any of it is sent can still be stored by a destination whose answer then times out. Answer that from
`#wrote_nothing?`, for `#log` and `#batch` alike.

Such a `#batch` works with any formatter, including a formatter block. An appender that cannot be
batched in some configuration says why from `#batch_refusal`, and what to do instead, so that
`add_appender` raises an `ArgumentError` with it when asked to batch the appender, with
`batch: true` or by default, rather than add an appender that writes nothing. It returns `nil`, by
default, when the appender can be batched. For example, a `#batch` that formats the whole batch with
`format_batch(logs)` needs a formatter that implements `#batch(logs, logger)`, so return
`format_batch_refusal`, which says whether the appender's formatter can format a batch:

~~~ruby
def batch(logs)
  client.send_request(format_batch(logs))
end

def batch_refusal
  format_batch_refusal
end
~~~

Like `format_log` and `format_batch`, `format_batch_refusal` is a private helper of
