Rack -- Started -- {:ip => "127.0.0.1", :method => "GET", :path => "/assets/application.css"}
~~~

To silence them:

~~~ruby
config.rails_semantic_logger.quiet_assets = true
~~~

### Color output

Color is chosen per appender with the `formatter:` option: use `:color` for colorized output and
`:default` for plain text (see [Output formats](#output-formats)). For example, color on screen and
plain text in a file:

~~~ruby
config.rails_semantic_logger.appenders do |appenders|
  appenders.add(file_name: "log/#{Rails.env}.log", formatter: :default)
  appenders.add_server(formatter: :color)
end
~~~

The Rails `config.colorize_logging` setting does **not** affect appenders declared in the block; it
only influences the deprecated default file appender (see
[Deprecated configuration options](#deprecated-configuration-options)).

### Named tags

Add tags to every log entry on a per-request basis by setting `config.log_tags` to a Hash:

~~~ruby
config.log_tags = {
  request_id: :request_id,
  ip:         :remote_ip,
  user:       ->(request) { request.cookie_jar["login"] }
}
~~~

Notes:

* If a value returns `nil`, that key is omitted for that request.
* To turn named tags off in development, set `config.log_tags = nil` in
  `config/environments/development.rb`.
* The tags are computed when the request enters the middleware stack, before the session is loaded
  and before authentication middleware such as Warden (used by Devise) runs. A value can come from
  the request's headers or cookies, but not from the signed-in user.

#### Tag a request with the signed-in user

To tag every entry logged while a controller handles a request with values that are only known
inside the controller, such as the signed-in user, wrap the action in an `around_action`:

~~~ruby
class ApplicationController < ActionController::Base
  around_action :tag_logs

  private

  def tag_logs(&)
    SemanticLogger.tagged({user_id: current_user&.id}.compact, &)
  end
end
~~~

The tags apply until the action finishes, and are removed even when it raises an exception. The
`compact` leaves the tag out for a request without a signed-in user. The tags are not on the
`Started`, `Processing`, and `Completed` entries, which are logged outside the action's callbacks. To
add the user to the `Completed` entry as well, see
[Add custom data to the Completed message](#add-custom-data-to-the-completed-message).

Use the block form, as above, rather than `SemanticLogger.push_named_tags` in a `before_action`.
Tags added with `push_tags` or `push_named_tags` stay on the thread until they are popped, and web
servers such as Puma serve many requests on each thread, so tags pushed during one request would be
logged for every later request on that thread.

When a nested block sets a named tag that is already set, its value replaces the earlier one. A
Hash value, such as `user: {id: 1}`, is replaced as a whole rather than merged with the earlier
Hash, so prefer flat keys such as `user_id:`.

### Source file name, line number, and method

In development, Rails Semantic Logger records the file, line number, and method of the code behind
each entry, at every level. In the Rails console it records them for each entry at the console's log
level, in every environment.

~~~
2026-11-15 13:58:05.906754 I [8462:puma srv tp 001 orders_controller.rb:12 OrdersController#create] OrdersController -- Creating order
~~~

To record them in another environment, or only at and above a level, set that level:

~~~ruby
config.semantic_logger.call_site_level = :info
~~~

To stop recording them in development, set it to `nil` in `config/application.rb`,
`config/environments/development.rb`, or an initializer:

~~~ruby
config.semantic_logger.call_site_level = nil
~~~

This reads only the stack frames up to the code that made the log call, so it is cheap enough to
leave on in production. See
[Recording where each entry was logged](config.html#recording-where-each-entry-was-logged) for its
cost, and for which formatters write it.

Rails logs the entries for its own events from Active Support's notifications, so the code that makes
their log call is Active Support's. Rails Semantic Logger records the application code behind each
one instead:

| Entry | Call site |
|-------|-----------|
| SQL query, strict loading violation | The code that ran the query |
| `Redirected to`, `Sent data`, `Sent file`, unpermitted parameters, fragment caching | The line in the action |
| `Processing`, `Completed`, CSRF warnings | The controller's action |
| `rescue_from` | Where the exception was raised |
| `Rendering`, `Rendered` | The code that called `render`, or the template that rendered a partial |
| Active Job | The code that enqueued or performed the job, or else the job's `#perform`, as for a job that a worker, or the inline or test adapter, performs from its queue |
| Action Mailer | The code that delivered the mail, or else the mailer's action |
| An exception that a request raised | Where your code raised it |

Entries with no application code behind them record no call site: `Started`, a halted filter chain,
a template that Rails renders once the action has returned, and the entries of Sidekiq's and Solid
Queue's own processes. Code that only wraps what Rails runs, such as an `around_action` or a
worker's middleware, is not taken for the code behind an entry that Rails logs once it has taken over
from your code, as it does to render an action's template, or to perform a job from its queue. The
application code is the first frame that the subscriber's `backtrace_cleaner` keeps,
`Rails.backtrace_cleaner` unless you assign another, such as
`RailsSemanticLogger::ActiveRecord::LogSubscriber.backtrace_cleaner`. It is also the `source` that
`config.active_record.verbose_query_logs` and `config.active_job.verbose_enqueue_logs` add to the
payload.

To capture the whole backtrace of each entry instead, use `backtrace_level`:

~~~ruby
config.semantic_logger.backtrace_level = :info
~~~


**Warning:** capturing a backtrace for every log entry allocates many objects. In production set this
to `nil` (disabled) or to a high level such as `:error`. By default backtraces are only captured for
`:error` and `:fatal`. This feature is best used in development.

### Cleaning exception backtraces

Rails Semantic Logger cleans the backtraces of logged exceptions with `Rails.backtrace_cleaner`, as
Rails' own log does: only your application's frames are logged, relative to `Rails.root`. The
silencers and filters added in `config/initializers/backtrace_silencers.rb` apply, since they change
the same cleaner. Set the `BACKTRACE` environment variable to log full backtraces again, as with the
rest of Rails.

The text and JSON formatters use it, including the JSON sent by the HTTP, Elasticsearch HTTP, TCP,
UDP, Kafka, RabbitMQ, and CloudWatch Logs appenders. Error services, such as Sentry, still receive
the full backtrace. When none of an exception's frames is your application's, such as one raised
entirely within a gem, the full backtrace is logged.

A request for a missing route, and the other exceptions that Rails logs without a backtrace when
none of its frames is your application's (those in `ActionDispatch::ExceptionWrapper.silent_exceptions`),
is logged on one line, after the response's status, as in Rails' own log:

~~~
Rails -- 404 Not Found -- Exception: ActionController::RoutingError: No route matches [GET] "/apple-touch-icon.png"
~~~

That entry has the exception's class and message, and names the exceptions that caused it, which
Rails lists as "Caused by", but not the exception itself (`log_exception: :partial`): the `:json`
formatter writes them in its `message`, and Semantic Logger's own error service appenders, such as
`sentry_ruby`, receive a message rather than an exception. Error services hooked into Rails still receive the exception. Set `BACKTRACE` to log
these with their backtrace, or set `config.action_dispatch.log_rescued_responses = false` to leave
them out of the log.

To use another cleaner, or none, assign it in `config/application.rb`. This does not change how the
exceptions above are logged:

~~~ruby
config.semantic_logger.backtrace_cleaner = nil
~~~

See [Cleaning backtraces](config.html#cleaning-backtraces) for which formatters use it, and how to
choose for one appender.

### Redacting sensitive data

Rails filters `config.filter_parameters` only from the request parameters that it logs. Rails Semantic
Logger also has Semantic Logger redact them from every log entry: the value of each key that they
match is written as `"[FILTERED]"`, at any depth, in the payload, named tags, and context, by every
appender. That covers your own calls, such as `logger.info("Charged", card: card_params)`, and the
entries of other gems, as well as Rails' own. The filters are read once the application has
initialized, so those in `config/initializers/filter_parameter_logging.rb` apply.

Keys are matched by name, both as written and in snake_case, so `:_key` also matches an `X-Api-Key`
header, as `x_api_key`. A filter matches any key that contains it, so the default list of a new Rails
application (`:passw, :email, :secret, :token, :_key, :crypt, :salt, :certificate, :otp, :ssn, :cvv,
:cvc`) also redacts keys that are not secret, such as `max_tokens`, `token_count`, `cache_key`, and
`api_key_id`, the `concurrency_key` of Solid Queue's entries, and every `email`.

That list does not match the `Authorization` or `Cookie` header. Add them:

~~~ruby
# config/initializers/filter_parameter_logging.rb
Rails.application.config.filter_parameters += %i[authorization cookie]
~~~

What is not redacted:

* Active Job `arguments` and Action Mailer `args`, which are logged as JSON text. For a job that takes
  a secret, leave its arguments out of the log with `self.log_arguments = false`.
* A key that only a Proc filter matches: a Proc changes a value rather than naming a key, so it is
  left out.
* A key nested under the one a dotted filter names. A filter such as `"credit_card.code"` only
  matches a key with that whole name, not `code` inside `credit_card`. That includes the
  `"model.attribute"` filters that Rails adds for Active Record encrypted attributes.
* The message, plain tags, and exception messages: only keyed data is redacted.
* Entries logged while the application starts, before the list is complete.

To use other keys instead, assign them in `config/application.rb`, and Rails Semantic Logger keeps
them:

~~~ruby
config.semantic_logger.sensitive_keys = %i[passw secret token _key authorization cookie]
~~~

To turn redaction off:

~~~ruby
config.rails_semantic_logger.redact_filter_parameters = false
~~~

Assigning `config.semantic_logger.sensitive_keys = nil` does not turn it off, since that cannot be
told apart from never assigning it. See [Redacting sensitive data](security.html#redacting-sensitive-data)
for what `sensitive_keys` accepts, and when redaction runs.

### Add custom data to the Completed message

Add an `append_info_to_payload` method to a controller to include extra fields in its Completed
message:

~~~ruby
class ThingController < ApplicationController
  private

  def append_info_to_payload(payload)
    super
    payload[:user_id] = current_user&.id
  end
end
~~~

### Customize the Completed message text

Provide a Proc to build the Action Controller message from the message and payload:

~~~ruby
config.rails_semantic_logger.action_message_format = ->(message, payload) do
  "#{message} - #{payload[:controller]}##{payload[:action]}"
end
~~~

### Background job loggers

By default Rails Semantic Logger replaces the Sidekiq and SolidQueue loggers. To leave them alone:

~~~ruby
config.rails_semantic_logger.replace_sidekiq_logger     = false
config.rails_semantic_logger.replace_solid_queue_logger = false
~~~

Sidekiq v7 and v8 are supported. Earlier Sidekiq versions were supported up to
Rails Semantic Logger v5.0.

#### Sidekiq job lifecycle messages

For every Sidekiq job, Rails Semantic Logger emits a `Start #perform` and a `Completed #perform`
entry (with the `sidekiq.queue.latency` and `sidekiq.job.perform` metrics). On very high job volumes
these can add noise and cost in log aggregation tools. To turn them off (the job still runs and any
exceptions are still logged):

~~~ruby
# config/initializers/sidekiq.rb
RailsSemanticLogger::Sidekiq::JobLogger.perform_messages = false
~~~

This defaults to `true`, so the messages are emitted unless you opt out.

On Sidekiq 8, the standard Sidekiq setting has the same effect and is also honored:

~~~ruby
Sidekiq.configure_server do |config|
  config[:skip_default_job_logging] = true
end
~~~

#### Sidekiq job logging context

Every log entry emitted while a job runs is tagged with the job's `jid`, class, and queue, plus its
`bid` (batch id) and `tags` when present. On Sidekiq 8, the standard `logged_job_attributes` setting
is honored, so additional job attributes can be added to the logging context:

~~~ruby
Sidekiq.configure_server do |config|
  config[:logged_job_attributes] = %w[bid tags priority]
end
~~~

#### Testing Sidekiq jobs and middleware

Use the [test helpers](testing.html) (`capture_semantic_logger_events` in RSpec,
`semantic_logger_events` in Minitest) to capture the log events from jobs and server middleware. This
relies on `replace_sidekiq_logger` being on (the default): with it off, jobs and middleware log
through a plain `Sidekiq::Logger`, which the helpers do not capture.

Two things differ from a running Sidekiq server:

- Sidekiq's testing modes (`inline!`, and `fake!` with `drain` or `perform_one`) run only the
  middleware added to `Sidekiq::Testing.server_middleware`, not the chain from
  `Sidekiq.configure_server`. Add the middleware under test there.
- The job logger does not run, so there are no `Start #perform` or `Completed #perform` entries, and
  no `jid`, class, or queue named tags. Named tags added by your own middleware are still present.

Capture every event rather than one class's. Middleware that includes `Sidekiq::ServerMiddleware`
logs through Sidekiq's configured logger, which a capture scoped to a class, such as
`capture_semantic_logger_events(Sidekiq)`, does not reach.

The example below turns on Sidekiq's testing modes with `Sidekiq.testing!(:fake)`, available from
Sidekiq 8.1.1. On earlier versions use `require "sidekiq/testing"` instead.

~~~ruby
# spec/rails_helper.rb
Sidekiq.testing!(:fake)

# app/sidekiq/tenant_logging_middleware.rb
class TenantLoggingMiddleware
  include Sidekiq::ServerMiddleware

  def call(_job_instance, job, _queue, &block)
    SemanticLogger.tagged(tenant: job["tenant"], &block)
  end
end

# app/sidekiq/report_job.rb
class ReportJob
  include Sidekiq::Job

  def perform
    logger.info("Building report")
  end
end

# spec/sidekiq/tenant_logging_middleware_spec.rb
RSpec.describe TenantLoggingMiddleware do
  around { |example| Sidekiq::Testing.inline! { example.run } }
  before { Sidekiq::Testing.server_middleware { |chain| chain.add TenantLoggingMiddleware } }
  after  { Sidekiq::Testing.server_middleware { |chain| chain.remove TenantLoggingMiddleware } }

  it "tags the job's log entries with the tenant" do
    events = capture_semantic_logger_events { ReportJob.set(tenant: "acme").perform_async }
    event  = events.find { |e| e.name == "ReportJob" }

    expect(event).to be_a_semantic_logger_event(message: "Building report")
    expect(event.named_tags).to include(tenant: "acme")
  end
end
~~~

The last line checks only the `tenant` tag, so the test still passes when other named tags are
active.

### Custom controller base class

If your application uses a controller base class other than `ActionController::Base` or
`ActionController::API`, Rails Semantic Logger falls back to the `ActionController::Base` logger, so
those entries are named `ActionController::Base`. To give them the correct class name, include the
mixin in your base class:

~~~ruby
include SemanticLogger::Loggable
~~~

If the base class lives in a third-party gem, do it from an initializer:

~~~ruby
CustomControllerBase.include(SemanticLogger::Loggable)
~~~

---

## Metrics (prototype)

> **Prototype:** metrics support and the metric names below are an early prototype and **subject to
> change** in a future release. Do not hard-code these names into long-lived dashboards or alerts yet.

In addition to the structured log entry, Rails Semantic Logger attaches a Semantic Logger
[metric](metrics.html) to each entry that is logged at `:info`, `:warn`, or `:error`. When the entry
carries a duration (a request, query, render, job run, ...) the metric records that timing; otherwise
it acts as an event counter. Wire up a metrics appender (StatsD, Prometheus, ...) and these flow
through automatically alongside the logs.

Metric names follow `rails.<component>.<event>`, where `<component>` is the Rails component with its
`action_`/`active_` prefix dropped:

| Component | Metrics |
| --- | --- |
| Action Controller | `rails.controller.process_action`, `rails.controller.send_file`, `rails.controller.send_data`, `rails.controller.redirect_to`, `rails.controller.halted_callback`, `rails.controller.rescue_from_callback`, and the fragment-cache events (`rails.controller.write_fragment`, `read_fragment`, `exist_fragment`, `expire_fragment`, `expire_page`, `write_page`) |
| Action View | `rails.view.render.template`, `rails.view.render.partial`, `rails.view.render.layout`, `rails.view.render.collection` |
| Active Job | `rails.job.<event>` for every job event (`enqueue`, `enqueue_at`, `enqueue_all`, `perform_start`, `perform`, `enqueue_retry`, `retry_stopped`, `discard`, and the Rails 8.1 Continuation events `interrupt`, `resume`, `step_skipped`, `step_started`, `step`) |
| Action Mailer | `rails.mailer.deliver` |
| Solid Queue | `rails.solid_queue.<event>` for every Solid Queue event logged at info/warn/error (e.g. `rails.solid_queue.start_process`, `rails.solid_queue.thread_error`) |

Entries logged at `:debug` carry **no** metric. Because ActiveRecord logs SQL at `:debug`, there is
currently no `rails.db`/`rails.record` SQL metric, and Action View render metrics are only emitted
when rendered events are raised to `:info` (see
[Re-enable Started, Processing, and Rendered messages](#re-enable-started-processing-and-rendered-messages)).

---

## Operational notes

### Process forking

If you use a forking server (Puma, Unicorn) or fork worker processes, see
[Process Forking](operations.html#process-forking). With Semantic Logger v5 appenders are reopened automatically after
a fork, so the manual `after_fork { SemanticLogger.reopen }` hook is usually no longer needed.

### Drop messages instead of blocking

By default, if log messages arrive faster than the appenders can write them, calls to `logger.info`
wait once the in-memory queue is full, so requests, jobs, and shutdown hooks that log can stall behind
a slow destination. When staying responsive matters more than keeping every message, have them dropped
instead, in `config/application.rb` or `config/environments/production.rb`:

~~~ruby
config.semantic_logger.non_blocking = true
~~~

This needs Semantic Logger v5.2 or later. See
[Drop messages instead of blocking](operations.html#drop-messages-instead-of-blocking) for how it
relates to the per-appender `non_blocking:` option and how dropped messages are reported.

### Log rotation

Because the log file is held open between writes, rotate it with a **copy-truncate** strategy rather
than deleting and recreating the file. Example `logrotate` configuration for Linux:

~~~
/var/www/my_app/shared/log/*.log {
  daily
  missingok
  copytruncate
  rotate 14
  compress
  delaycompress
  notifempty
}
~~~

### Loggers that are replaced automatically

After they initialize, Rails Semantic Logger replaces the loggers of these libraries when present:

- Action Cable
- Bugsnag
- Delayed Job
- IOStreams
- Mongo
- Mongoid
- Moped
- Resque
- Sidekiq (unless `replace_sidekiq_logger = false`)
- Sidetiq
- Solid Queue (unless `replace_solid_queue_logger = false`)

---

## Upgrading to v5.3

v5.3 requires Semantic Logger v5.3; see [Upgrading to Semantic Logger v5.3](upgrading.html#upgrading-to-semantic-logger-v53)
for the changes there. It needs no configuration changes, but several log entries change. Review
these before you upgrade if a log query, dashboard, or alert depends on them.

### Exception backtraces are cleaned

The backtraces of logged exceptions are now cleaned with `Rails.backtrace_cleaner`, as in Rails' own
log: only your application's frames are written, relative to `Rails.root`. Error services, such as
Sentry, still receive the full backtrace. To log full backtraces again, set the `BACKTRACE`
environment variable, or turn cleaning off in `config/application.rb`:

~~~ruby
config.semantic_logger.backtrace_cleaner = nil
~~~

A request for a missing route, and the other exceptions in
`ActionDispatch::ExceptionWrapper.silent_exceptions`, is now logged on one line, without the exception
itself, when none of its frames is your application's. Semantic Logger's own error service appenders,
such as `sentry_ruby`, therefore receive a message for it rather than an exception. See
[Cleaning exception backtraces](#cleaning-exception-backtraces).

### `config.filter_parameters` are redacted from every entry

The keys in `config.filter_parameters` are now redacted from the payload, named tags, and context of
every log entry, not only from the request parameters. A filter matches any key that contains it, so
Rails' default filters also redact keys such as `email`, `max_tokens`, `cache_key`, and
`api_key_id`. Rails' defaults do not match the `Authorization` or `Cookie` headers, so consider adding
them. To turn redaction off:

~~~ruby
config.rails_semantic_logger.redact_filter_parameters = false
~~~

See [Redacting sensitive data](#redacting-sensitive-data).

### Call sites are recorded in development

In development, each entry now records the file, line, and method of the code behind it. The text
formatters write it after the thread name, and the `:json` formatter as `file`, `line`, and `method`.
In the Rails console it replaces capturing a backtrace for every entry. To turn it off:

~~~ruby
config.semantic_logger.call_site_level = nil
~~~

See [Source file name, line number, and method](#source-file-name-line-number-and-method).

### Other log output changes

* Active Record: SQL bind values that have no column name are keyed by position (`$1`, `$2`, ...),
  as in Rails 8.2's own log, instead of all under a `nil` key. Update anything that matches
  `payload.binds.nil`.
* Active Job: the message of an enqueue that failed now closes its parentheses:
  `Failed enqueuing MyJob (Job ID: 1a2b) to Sidekiq(default): RuntimeError (boom)`.
* Action Controller: the `source` of a `Redirected to` entry, written when
  `ActionDispatch.verbose_redirect_logs` is on, is now relative to `Rails.root` instead of an absolute
  path.
* `config.active_record.verbose_query_logs` and `config.active_job.verbose_enqueue_logs`, which new
  Rails applications turn on in development, are now honored: query and enqueue entries gain a
  `source` in their payload.
* Rails 8.1+: open redirects and path relative redirects reported with `:notify` are now logged at
  `:warn`. On Rails 8.2, CSRF failures are logged at `:warn` again.

See the [CHANGELOG](https://github.com/reidmorrison/rails_semantic_logger/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md)
for the full list, including Rails 8.2 support.

---

## Upgrading to v5.1

v5.1 requires Semantic Logger v5.1 and needs no configuration changes. Two behaviors differ.

### A log file that cannot be opened now fails at boot

Semantic Logger v5.1 opens the file appender's log file when the appender is created, rather than on
the first write. A missing directory, a bad path, or insufficient permissions therefore raises
during boot, where Rails Semantic Logger catches it and falls back to logging to standard error at
the `:warn` level, with a message explaining the problem.

Previously that failure surfaced asynchronously on the appender thread after the application had
already booted, so the fallback never ran and the app kept running against an appender that silently
dropped every message. If you have been running with an unwritable log path without noticing, this
release is when you will find out.

As a side effect, the log file is created as soon as the appender is added, even if nothing has been
logged yet. This matches the standard Ruby and Rails loggers.

### Sidekiq v4, v5, and v6 are no longer supported

Sidekiq v7 and v8 are supported and tested. The patches for older versions have been removed, along
with the pre-7.1.6 error handler branches. Sidekiq v7 and v8 both predate this gem's Rails 7.2 and
Ruby 3.2 minimums, so upgrading Sidekiq is the path forward.

On Sidekiq 8 two of its own settings are now honored: `logged_job_attributes` adds job attributes to
the logging context, and `skip_default_job_logging` suppresses the `Start #perform` /
`Completed #perform` messages (an alternative to
`RailsSemanticLogger::Sidekiq::JobLogger.perform_messages = false`). See
[Sidekiq](#sidekiq) for the logging configuration.

---

## Migrating from v4 to v5

### Ruby and Rails minimums

v5 requires Ruby 3.2+ and Rails 7.2+. It also depends on Semantic Logger v5; review the
[Semantic Logger upgrade notes](upgrading.html) for changes there (the most relevant for Rails apps
is that appenders are now reopened automatically after fork, so you can remove manual reopen hooks).

### Appender configuration is the main change

In v4 the log file, its format, and any extra destinations were configured through several separate
options (`format`, `add_file_appender`, `ap_options`, `filter`, `console_logger`) plus direct
`config.semantic_logger.add_appender(...)` calls. In v5 all of that lives in one place, the
[appenders block](#configuring-where-logs-go-the-appenders-block).

These v4 options still work in v5 but emit a deprecation warning and will be **removed in v6**.
Migrate them as follows:

| v4 | v5 |
|----|----|
| `config.rails_semantic_logger.format = :json` | `appenders.add(file_name: "log/#{Rails.env}.log", formatter: :json)` |
| `config.rails_semantic_logger.add_file_appender = false` then `config.semantic_logger.add_appender(...)` | Declare your destinations with `appenders.add(...)` (declaring any appender already replaces the default file appender) |
| `config.rails_semantic_logger.ap_options = {multiline: false}` | `appenders.add(..., formatter: {color: {ap: {multiline: false}}})` |
| `config.rails_semantic_logger.filter = /MyClass/` | `appenders.add(..., filter: /MyClass/)` |
| `config.rails_semantic_logger.console_logger = false` | Omit `add_console` (declare a console appender only if you want one) |

A v4 Heroku / standard-out configuration like:

~~~ruby
# v4
if ENV["RAILS_LOG_TO_STDOUT"].present?
  $stdout.sync = true
  config.rails_semantic_logger.add_file_appender = false
  config.semantic_logger.add_appender(io: $stdout, formatter: config.rails_semantic_logger.format)
end
~~~

becomes, in v5:

~~~ruby
# v5
config.rails_semantic_logger.appenders do |appenders|
  appenders.add(io: $stdout, formatter: :json)
end
~~~

### Server standard-out behavior

In v4, running `rails server` always added a standard-out logger, which you suppressed with
`bin/rails s --daemon` or Puma's `--quiet`. In v5 this is the job of `add_server`: when you use the
appenders block, declare an `add_server` appender to log to the screen while serving, or omit it to
stay silent. If you do not use the appenders block at all, the v4 behavior is preserved.

---

## Migrating from earlier versions

These notes apply to upgrades between older releases and are retained for reference.

### v4.16: Sidekiq metrics support

Rails Semantic Logger added support for Sidekiq metrics, available when the JSON logging format is
used:

* `sidekiq.job.perform` &mdash; the duration of each Sidekiq job; `duration` contains the time in
  milliseconds that the job took to run.
* `sidekiq.queue.latency` &mdash; the time between when a Sidekiq job was enqueued and when it was
  started; `metric_amount` contains the time in milliseconds that the job was waiting in the queue.

### v4.15 and v4.16: Sidekiq support

Rails Semantic Logger introduced direct support for Sidekiq v4, v5, v6, and v7. Remove any previous
custom patches or configurations used to make Sidekiq work with Semantic Logger. To see the complete
list of patches and to contribute your own, see
[Sidekiq Patches](https://github.com/reidmorrison/rails_semantic_logger/blob/v5.0.0/lib/rails_semantic_logger/extensions/sidekiq/sidekiq.rb).
Support for Sidekiq v4, v5, and v6 ended after Rails Semantic Logger v5.0; Sidekiq v7 and v8 are
supported and tested.

### v4.4

With some forking frameworks it was necessary to call `reopen` after the fork. As of v4.4 the
workaround for Ruby 2.5 crashes is no longer needed. Remove the following line if it is called
anywhere:

~~~ruby
SemanticLogger::Processor.instance.instance_variable_set(:@queue, Queue.new)
~~~

---

## Deprecated configuration options

The following options still function in v5 for backward compatibility but emit deprecation warnings
and will be **removed in v6**. Each is replaced by the [appenders block](#configuring-where-logs-go-the-appenders-block).

| Deprecated option | Replacement |
|-------------------|-------------|
| `config.rails_semantic_logger.format` | `formatter:` on each appender, e.g. `appenders.add(file_name: ..., formatter: :json)` |
| `config.rails_semantic_logger.ap_options` | `formatter: {color: {ap: {...}}}` on the appender |
| `config.rails_semantic_logger.filter` | `filter:` on the appender |
| `config.rails_semantic_logger.console_logger` | Declare (or omit) an `add_console` appender |
| `config.rails_semantic_logger.add_file_appender` | Declare appenders in the block (doing so already replaces the default file appender) |

### Silencing the warnings until you migrate

The gem registers its deprecator with the application as
`Rails.application.deprecators[:rails_semantic_logger]`, so the standard Rails deprecation settings
govern these warnings:

~~~ruby
# Hide them until you have migrated
config.active_support.report_deprecations = false

# Or silence only this gem's warnings, leaving the rest of the application's in place
Rails.application.deprecators[:rails_semantic_logger].silenced = true

# Or make them fatal, e.g. in config/environments/test.rb, so CI catches them
config.active_support.deprecation = :raise
~~~

The warnings are recorded when the option is set and emitted once Rails has applied the settings
above. Rails reads `config/environments/*.rb` well before it applies deprecation configuration, so
warning from the option setter itself would land where none of these settings could reach it. Each
option is reported once per boot, attributed to the place it was set. Options set later, from
`config/initializers/*` or at runtime, warn immediately instead.


---

<!-- source: docs/testing.md -->

## Testing

When testing application code, you often want to assert that it logged the right thing: the expected
message, level, payload, or metric. Semantic Logger logs through a global, asynchronous pipeline, so
you cannot simply read it back from a normal appender. Instead it ships a test helper that **captures
log events in memory** during a block, so you can make assertions on them.

The events are captured as raw `SemanticLogger::Log` objects, before any appender or formatter runs,
so your assertions are not affected by how logging happens to be configured.

Helpers are provided for both Minitest and RSpec. Other frameworks are covered further down.

## Minitest

### Step 1: install the helpers

Add the helper methods to your tests, once, in `test_helper.rb`:

~~~ruby
Minitest::Test.include SemanticLogger::Test::Minitest
~~~

### Step 2: capture events

Wrap the code under test in `semantic_logger_events`. It returns every log event created during the
block:

~~~ruby
messages = semantic_logger_events do
  User.new.enable!
end
~~~

By default it captures events from every class. To capture only the events from one class, pass that
class as `klass:`:

~~~ruby
messages = semantic_logger_events(klass: ApiClient) do
  # Only ApiClient log events created during this block are captured.
end
~~~

Passing a class replaces that class's `logger` while the block runs, so it captures only the log calls
made through that logger. Capture without a class instead when:

- the code under test logs through a logger it got some other way, such as `SemanticLogger["Name"]`
  or a logger handed to it by a framework;
- an instance of the class called `logger` before the block, since each instance keeps the first
  logger it is given; or
- you need to assert on `name`: events captured through a class are named
  `SemanticLogger::Test::CaptureLogEvents`, not after the class.

### Step 3: assert on the events

Check how many events were produced, then assert on each one with `assert_semantic_logger_event`:

~~~ruby
require_relative "test_helper"

class UserTest < ActiveSupport::TestCase
  describe User do
    it "logs message" do
      messages = semantic_logger_events do
        User.new.enable!
      end

      # How many events were logged
      assert_equal 2, messages.count, messages

      # The first event
      assert_semantic_logger_event(
        messages[0],
        level:   :info,
        message: "User enabled"
      )

      # The second event
      assert_semantic_logger_event(
        messages[1],
        level:   :debug,
        message: "Completed"
      )
    end
  end
end
~~~

Every argument other than the event itself is optional, so you assert only on what matters to the
test. The available checks are:

| Argument | Checks |
|----------|--------|
| `message` | Exact match of the text message. |
| `message_includes` | Partial (substring) match of the message. |
| `level` | Log level: `:trace`, `:debug`, `:info`, `:warn`, `:error`, `:fatal`. |
| `payload` | Exact match of the payload Hash. |
| `payload_includes` | Partial match: the given keys/values, ignoring any others. |
| `tags` | Tags active on the thread when logged. |
| `named_tags` | Named tags active on the thread when logged. |
| `name` | Class name of the logger. |
| `exception` | The Ruby exception that was logged. |
| `metric` | The metric name. |
| `metric_amount` | The metric amount. |
| `dimensions` | The metric dimensions. |
| `context` | Named contexts captured with the entry. |
| `time` | When the entry was created. |
| `duration` | Duration of a measure call, in milliseconds. |
| `backtrace` | The captured backtrace, if any. |
| `call_site` | Where the entry was logged, a `SemanticLogger::CallSite`, when `SemanticLogger.call_site_level` is set. |
| `thread_name` | Name of the thread that logged the entry, or its object id when the thread has no name. |

### Match part of a message or payload

For assertions that should not break on incidental detail, match partially.

Use `message_includes` for a substring of the message:

~~~ruby
assert_semantic_logger_event(
  messages[0],
  level:            :info,
  message_includes: "enabled"
)
~~~

Use `payload_includes` to assert specific payload keys while ignoring any extras. Compare with
`payload`, which must match the whole Hash exactly:

~~~ruby
# Exact: the payload must be exactly these keys and values
assert_semantic_logger_event(
  messages[0],
  level:   :info,
  message: "User enabled",
  payload: {first_name: "Jack", last_name: "Jones"}
)

# Partial: first_name must be present, other keys are ignored
assert_semantic_logger_event(
  messages[0],
  level:            :info,
  message:          "User enabled",
  payload_includes: {first_name: "Jack"}
)
~~~

For more examples, see the
[Rails Semantic Logger tests](https://github.com/reidmorrison/rails_semantic_logger/blob/main/test/active_record_test.rb).

## RSpec

The RSpec helpers mirror the Minitest ones: a capture helper plus matchers for asserting on the
captured events.

### Step 1: install the helpers

Require the helpers and include them, once, in `spec_helper.rb`:

~~~ruby
require "semantic_logger/test/rspec"

RSpec.configure do |config|
  config.include SemanticLogger::Test::RSpec
end
~~~

### Step 2: capture events

Wrap the code under test in `capture_semantic_logger_events`. It returns every log event created
during the block, regardless of the global default log level:

~~~ruby
events = capture_semantic_logger_events do
  User.new.enable!
end
~~~

By default it captures events from every class. To capture only the events from one class, pass that
class:

~~~ruby
events = capture_semantic_logger_events(ApiClient) do
  # Only ApiClient log events created during this block are captured.
end
~~~

Passing a class replaces that class's `logger` until the end of the example, not just the block, so
it captures only the log calls made through that logger. Log calls made after the block are added to
the same returned array, so check the event count before running more code that logs. Capture without
a class instead when:

- the code under test logs through a logger it got some other way, such as `SemanticLogger["Name"]`
  or a logger handed to it by a framework;
- an instance of the class called `logger` before the block, since each instance keeps the first
  logger it is given; or
- you need to assert on `name`: events captured through a class are named
  `SemanticLogger::Test::CaptureLogEvents`, not after the class.

### Step 3: assert on the events

Use `be_a_semantic_logger_event` to assert on a single captured event:

~~~ruby
RSpec.describe User do
  it "logs message" do
    events = capture_semantic_logger_events do
      User.new.enable!
    end

    expect(events.count).to eq(2)

    expect(events[0]).to be_a_semantic_logger_event(
      level:   :info,
      message: "User enabled"
    )

    expect(events[1]).to be_a_semantic_logger_event(
      level:   :debug,
      message: "Completed"
    )
  end
end
~~~

Every argument is optional, so you assert only on what matters to the test. The available checks are
the same as the [Minitest table above](#step-3-assert-on-the-events), plus `message_includes`,
`payload_includes`, and `exception_includes` for partial matches:

~~~ruby
expect(events[0]).to be_a_semantic_logger_event(
  level:            :info,
  message_includes: "enabled",
  payload_includes: {first_name: "Jack"}
)
~~~

An expected value that is a Class matches by type, and `:nil` asserts the attribute is `nil`:

~~~ruby
expect(events[0]).to be_a_semantic_logger_event(time: Time, exception: :nil)
~~~

### Match against a list of events

`a_semantic_logger_event` is a composable alias, so it works inside `include` and other matchers:

~~~ruby
expect(events).to include(
  a_semantic_logger_event(message: "User enabled")
)
~~~

### Assert directly on a block

`log_semantic_logger_event` captures the events for you and passes if any of them match. Pass `on:`
to capture only one class's events:

~~~ruby
expect { User.new.enable! }.to(
  log_semantic_logger_event(level: :info, message: "User enabled")
)

expect { ApiClient.new.call }.to(
  log_semantic_logger_event(on: ApiClient, metric: "ApiClient/call")
)
~~~

## Metrics

The same helpers capture the metric calls (`increment`, `time`, `record`, and the `metric:` of log
and `measure_*` calls) as they are made, whether or not a metric appender is present, and whatever
the log level. `semantic_logger_metrics` and `assert_metric` for Minitest:

~~~ruby
metrics = semantic_logger_metrics { Signup.new.call(user) }
assert_metric(metrics, name: "users.signup", kind: :counter, value: 1)
assert_metric(metrics, name: "supplier.add_user", kind: :histogram, unit: "s", value: Float)
~~~

`capture_semantic_logger_metrics`, `a_semantic_logger_metric`, `be_a_semantic_logger_metric`, and
`record_semantic_logger_metric` for RSpec:

~~~ruby
expect { Signup.new.call(user) }.to(
  record_semantic_logger_metric(name: "users.signup", kind: :counter, value: 1)
)
~~~

See [Test metrics](metrics.html#test-metrics) for the details.

## Other test frameworks

The same approach works anywhere: replace the logger with a
`SemanticLogger::Test::CaptureLogEvents` instance. It looks and behaves like a normal logger, but
keeps the raw log events in memory instead of writing them, so your assertions are unaffected by the
configured appenders or their formats.

~~~ruby
logger = SemanticLogger::Test::CaptureLogEvents.new
~~~

Stub it onto a single class to capture just that class's logging:

~~~ruby
User.stub(:logger, logger) do
  # Capture all logging calls to the User logger.
end
~~~

Or stub the global processor to capture logging from every class:

~~~ruby
SemanticLogger::Logger.stub(:processor, logger) do
  # Capture all log events during the block.
end
~~~

Either way, the captured events are available as `logger.events`, and the metric calls as
`logger.metric_events`.

If you add helper methods for another framework like the Minitest ones, a pull request would be
welcome.


---

<!-- source: docs/operations.md -->

## Operations

This page covers running Semantic Logger in production: keeping logging alive across process forks,
rotating log files, tuning the background pipeline, controlling a running process with signals, and
shipping logs to a centralized system. The defaults are good for most applications, so reach for
these topics when you have a specific operational need.

For first-time setup (global settings, appenders, formatters, and filtering), see
[Configuration](config.html).

## Process forking

Frameworks such as Puma, Unicorn, and Resque **fork** the process: they start a worker by cloning the
parent. A forked child does not inherit a working copy of the parent's log file handles or background
thread, so unless those are re-opened in the child, logging quietly stops.

### It is automatic (default)

As of v5 you do not need to do anything. Semantic Logger installs a `Process._fork` hook (Ruby 3.1
and later) that calls `SemanticLogger.reopen` in the child after `fork`, `Process.fork`,
`Process.daemon`, and `IO.popen("-")`, the calls that fork the Ruby process. That covers every
forking framework (Puma, Unicorn, Resque, Spring, Phusion Passenger, parallel tests, and so on).
`Kernel#system`, backticks, `spawn`, and `IO.popen` with a command start another program instead,
which has nothing to reopen. The process can also fork in a signal trap.

`reopen` runs only once per process after a fork, so it is safe even if something else also calls it.

Each appender is reopened by the thread that writes its entries, before it writes the next one, so
that an appender is never reopened while it is writing (see [Reopen manually](#reopen-manually)).
After a fork, that is the child's own thread, which reopens the appender before it writes anything.

In the child, the appenders that keep a connection open to their server leave the one they inherited
to the parent, without closing it or writing to it, and connect again: `:http` and the appenders
built on it (`:elasticsearch_http`, `:splunk_http`, `:loki`, `metric: :otlp`, and
`metric: :signalfx`), `:tcp`, `:syslog` and `:graylog` over TCP, `:kafka`, and `:rabbitmq`. Closing a TLS connection sends the
server a `close_notify`, which ends the connection for the parent too, and over TLS the server
cannot read what the parent writes after the child has written to it. When one of them cannot
connect in the child, such as while its server cannot be reached, it connects before it writes the
next entry. They also leave the connection they inherited to the parent when they are closed in the
child before they have reopened, such as with `SemanticLogger.reopen_on_fork = false`.
`SemanticLogger.remove_appender` in the child first waits, when the thread that writes the entries
has not yet reopened the appenders, until it has, so that the appender it removes closes only what
the child built. That matters for an appender of your own whose `#reopen` leaves the connection it
inherited to the parent, but whose `#close` closes whatever connection it holds.
(`:kafka` connects only when it delivers; when it cannot build a new producer in the child, such as
for invalid options, logging to it raises `IOError` until it is reopened.)

`:cloudwatch_logs` and `:mongodb` cannot do the same, since their gems keep their connections, and
still act on the parent's in the child. The AWS SDK keeps one pool of connections for all its
clients with the same options, so in the child it can reuse a connection the parent left idle in the
pool, and before each request it finishes those idle for longer than its `http_idle_timeout` (5
seconds by default), including the parent's. The MongoDB driver closes the parent's connections in the child, when the
child uses its client, and when the child collects the client's connection pool, or exits. Over TLS,
finishing or closing a connection sends the server a `close_notify`, which ends the connection for
the parent too. Closed in the child before it has reopened, `:cloudwatch_logs` leaves the buffered
entries it inherited to the parent, which sends them. Closed in the child, even once it has reopened
there, `:mongodb` forgets the client it inherited without closing it, since closing it would end
the parent's sessions on the server; reopening it then connects a new client.

An appender that cannot be reopened, such as `:udp` once its server's name no longer resolves, or
`:http` while its server cannot be reached, is reported to the internal logger, as
`Failed to re-open appender`, or `Async: Failed to reopen the appender` for one added with
`async: true` or in batches, and carries on with what it had, apart from a connection inherited from
the parent (see above). The other appenders are still reopened, and the thread that writes the
entries of an appender added with `async: true` or in batches is still started in the child, so its
entries are written, or discarded and counted like any other entry it cannot write (see
[Retry a failing appender](#retry-a-failing-appender)), rather than left on its queue.

### Reopen manually

You only need the steps below if you turned the automatic hook off, or you rotated logs in a way that
did not fork (see [Log rotation](#log-rotation)).

1. Disable the automatic hook during boot, if you want full manual control:

   ~~~ruby
   SemanticLogger.reopen_on_fork = false
   ~~~

2. Call `reopen` yourself after each fork, or after an in-process log rotation. Within the same
   process, pass `force: true` to bypass the once-per-process guard:

   ~~~ruby
   SemanticLogger.reopen              # after a fork
   SemanticLogger.reopen(force: true) # same process, e.g. after external log rotation
   ~~~

   Within the same process, `reopen` keeps the log entries that are still queued, and the thread
   that writes them keeps running. That thread is only started again if it has stopped, such as
   after `async_max_retries`. After a fork, the child starts with an empty queue, since the parent
   process writes the entries it had queued.

   Within the same process, the appenders close the file or the connection that a reopen replaces.
   `:syslog` and `:graylog` over TCP, `:udp`, and `:rabbitmq` connect again before they close the
   connection they had, and keep it when they cannot connect. `:cloudwatch_logs` shuts down the
   timer that sends its buffered entries, and keeps those entries for the new timer.

   `reopen` only asks for the appenders to be reopened: each one is reopened by the thread that
   writes its entries, before it writes the next one, so that a file is never closed, nor a
   connection ended, while an entry is being written to it. So `reopen` returns before the appenders
   have reopened; a `SemanticLogger.flush` after it returns once they have. An appender added in
   batches reopens before its next batch, which it writes at most `batch_seconds` later, or when it
   is flushed. An entry still queued when `reopen` is called can be written after the reopen, such
   as to the new log file. That also lets `reopen` be called from a signal trap, such as one that a
   log rotation tool signals, since no appender connects or locks anything there. In synchronous mode
   (see [Synchronous operation](#synchronous-operation)), `reopen` reopens on the calling thread each
   appender that has no thread of its own, or, in a signal trap, on a thread that the trap starts
   and waits for, at most one second; an appender added with `async: true` or in batches is still
   reopened by its own thread.

You might opt out if another library forks in ways you do not want to trigger a reopen, or you need
to control exactly when the appender thread restarts.

## The json gem's warning about binary text

json 2.8.0 through 3.0.x print this warning each time they serialize a binary String that holds
UTF-8, such as a response body or Base64-decoded text:

```
warning: JSON.generate: UTF-8 string passed as BINARY, this will raise an encoding error in json 3.0
```

Semantic Logger writes such text as UTF-8 with every json version, so with those versions it
prepends a module to Ruby's `Warning` when it is loaded. The module drops this one warning when it
comes from Semantic Logger serializing log data. Every other warning is passed on, and so is this
one from the application's own JSON, including JSON that an exception's `#message` builds. A
module that the application prepends to `Warning` after loading Semantic Logger, such as a test
helper that raises on warnings, sees the warning first. The module is not installed with json 3.1
and later, which raise on such a String instead (Semantic Logger then writes a converted copy),
or on JRuby.

## Payload text where no locale is set

Where no UTF-8 locale is set, as in cron jobs, many container images, and systems with no locale
configured (`LC_ALL`, `LC_CTYPE`, and `LANG` unset, or set to `C` or `POSIX`), CRuby's default
external encoding is US-ASCII. The text formatters (`:default`, `:color`, `:one_line`, `:syslog`,
and `%{payload}` in `:pattern`) write the payload with Ruby's `#inspect`, which then writes each
character outside ASCII as an escape:

```
2026-11-16 09:10:53.874476 I [86699:1312] Checkout -- José -- {name: "Jos\u00E9"}
```

The message, tags, and named tags whose values are Strings are written as they are. A named tag
whose value is an Array or a Hash is written with `#inspect`, and so is escaped as the payload is.
The JSON formatters are not affected, and neither are Rails applications, since Rails sets the
default external encoding to UTF-8 (`config.encoding`), nor JRuby, whose default is UTF-8.

To write these characters, run Ruby with a UTF-8 locale or default external encoding, for example:

```shell
export LC_ALL=C.UTF-8
# or
export RUBYOPT=-Eutf-8
```

or set `Encoding.default_external = Encoding::UTF_8` when the application starts. `LC_ALL`, then
`LC_CTYPE`, take precedence over `LANG`, so setting `LANG=C.UTF-8` is not enough when either is set
to `C` or `POSIX`.

## Log rotation

For performance the log file is **not** re-opened on every write, so a log file must be rotated with
a **copy-truncate** strategy (copy the file aside, then truncate the original in place). Deleting or
renaming the file would leave Semantic Logger writing to a handle that no longer points at the live
file.

Linux's `logrotate` does this well. To set it up:

1. Create a config file for your application, for example `/etc/logrotate.d/my_app`.
2. Point it at your log directory and include `copytruncate`. For daily rotation:

   ~~~
   /var/www/rails/my_app/log/*.log {
           daily
           missingok
           copytruncate
           rotate 14
           compress
           delaycompress
           notifempty
   }
   ~~~

   Or, to rotate by size for very high volume logging:

   ~~~
   /var/www/rails/my_app/log/*.log {
           size 2G
           missingok
           copytruncate
           rotate 7
           compress
           nodelaycompress
           notifempty
           dateformat .%Y%m%d
   }
   ~~~

Other rotation tools work too, as long as they use copy-truncate. If your tool cannot copy-truncate
and instead moves the file, reopen the handles in-process afterwards with
`SemanticLogger.reopen(force: true)` (see [Process forking](#process-forking)).

## Performance and reliability tuning

Every logger hands its events to one shared background thread through an in-memory queue. That thread
writes each event to every appender in turn, so the call to `logger.info` returns immediately. The
knobs below tune that pipeline. The defaults suit most applications; reach for a knob when you have a
specific throughput, availability, or reliability requirement.

### Drop messages instead of blocking

By default the queue is capped (`max_queue_size`, default `10,000`). When it fills (for example
because an appender cannot keep up), `logger.info` **blocks** until there is room, guaranteeing no
message is lost at the cost of briefly slowing the application.

There are two places a slow appender can hold up the application, and a `non_blocking` setting for
each.

**A slow appender that runs on its own thread.** An appender added with `async: true` (or a batching
appender) has a second queue of its own, between the main queue and that appender. Set
`non_blocking: true` on it so that, once its own queue is full, messages for that appender are
**dropped** instead of holding up the main thread:

~~~ruby
SemanticLogger.add_appender(
  file_name:                      "production.log",
  async:                          true,
  non_blocking:                   true,
  dropped_message_report_seconds: 60
)
~~~

The main thread never waits on that appender, so the main queue keeps draining and every other
appender still receives every message. Prefer this when you know which appender is slow, such as one
that writes to a remote service. Dropped messages are counted and reported to the internal logger at
most once every `dropped_message_report_seconds` (default `30`), and appear as `dropped` for that
appender in `SemanticLogger.stats[:appenders]`.

**Everything else.** The main queue still fills if an appender that is not async slows down (for
example `io: $stdout` writing to a pipe that is not being read), or if the main thread cannot keep up
with the volume of messages. Set `SemanticLogger.non_blocking = true` so that messages are
**dropped** instead of blocking `logger.info` once the main queue is full:

~~~ruby
SemanticLogger.non_blocking = true
~~~

This can be set at any time, before or after appenders are added. Dropped messages are reported to
the internal logger at most once every 30 seconds, and the count is available from
`SemanticLogger.stats[:dropped]`. It is not supported in synchronous mode (`SemanticLogger.sync!`),
which has no queue.

When the queue is full, a message logged in a signal trap, such as by the handlers of
[`add_signal_handler`](#linux-signals), is dropped, counted, and reported the same way, with the
report made just after the trap rather than in it.

Either setting keeps logging calls from blocking; neither makes `SemanticLogger.flush` return sooner.
A flush, including the one that runs automatically when the process exits, still waits for every
message already on the queue to be written, unless the destination of an appender added with
`async: true` or in batches fails meanwhile, or, at exit, that of any other appender (see
[Retry a failing appender](#retry-a-failing-appender)).

`non_blocking` applies only to a capped queue. An uncapped queue (`max_queue_size: -1`) never blocks
and never drops, but can grow without bound.

### Retry a failing appender

If an appender raises while the worker thread is writing, the thread logs the error and restarts, so
a transient failure (such as a brief network blip to a remote appender) does not permanently stop
logging. Each restart sleeps with an increasing back-off (1 second, then 2, ...), reset as soon as a
message is processed successfully. The messages logged meanwhile wait on the queue.

When the appender says that the write that failed wrote none of the message (or, when batching, of
the batch), and is worth trying again, the thread writes the same message or batch again after the
back-off, ahead of the messages on the queue. Once the destination has answered it with a failure
after it was written again 3 times, it is discarded, and the thread carries on with the next one
once it has backed off, so that a message the destination fails every time does not hold up the
others until the thread gives up. A write that never reached the destination, such as one that
could not connect, is not counted, so an outage loses no messages until the thread gives up. The
HTTP based appenders say so for a `408`, `429`, or `503` response, and for a request they could not
send because they could not connect to the server; see
[When the server does not accept a request](appenders.html#when-the-server-does-not-accept-a-request).
Otherwise the message or batch is discarded straight away, since writing it again could write some
of it twice, or would fail the same way, and the thread carries on with the next one once it has
backed off.

A message that fails because of its own content, rather than the destination, is discarded and the
thread carries on straight away, without backing off: for example a value the formatter cannot
serialize (a `JSON::GeneratorError`, `JSON::NestingError`, encoding error, or `FloatDomainError`).
When batching with an appender that sends the whole batch in a single request, such as the HTTP,
Loki, Splunk HTTP, Elasticsearch, and OpenSearch appenders, only that message is discarded and the
rest of the batch is still written. With an appender that may have written part
of the batch before failing, the whole batch is discarded, so that no message is written twice.

A message that fails with an error that writing it again cannot fix, such as a request the
destination refuses for its credentials or its url, is discarded straight away too, without backing
off, as one that fails because of its content. When the appender says that such an error would fail
any batch, whatever it holds, as the HTTP based appenders do for a `401`, `403`, or `404`, the whole
batch is discarded at once, rather than split up to find the messages at fault.

Whether its content or the destination was at fault, the first discarded message is reported to the
internal logger straight away, with its error. After that, the number discarded is reported, with the
latest error, at most once every `dropped_message_report_seconds` (default `30`). The total appears
as `failed` for that appender in `SemanticLogger.stats[:appenders]`.

A `JSON::ParserError`, such as from a destination that answered with an HTML error page, is a
problem with the destination, so the thread backs off as for any other error. The appender decides
which errors are caused by message content; see [Custom appenders](config.html#custom-appenders).
The HTTP based appenders decide by the status of the response; see
[When the server does not accept a request](appenders.html#when-the-server-does-not-accept-a-request).

After `async_max_retries` (default `100`) consecutive failed restarts the worker thread gives up,
rather than spinning forever on a persistent failure, and discards the message or batch it was
writing again. From then on new log messages for that
appender are dropped once its queue is full, instead of blocking the application. So is a message
already waiting for room on the full queue when the thread gives up, within a second, which lets the
thread that logged it carry on: normally the thread that writes to every appender. The messages
already on the queue are kept, and the dropped ones are counted as `dropped` for that appender in
`SemanticLogger.stats[:appenders]`:

~~~ruby
SemanticLogger.add_appender(
  appender:          :http,
  url:               "https://example.com/log",
  async:             true,
  async_max_retries: 20
)
~~~

Set `async_max_retries: -1` to retry indefinitely. The back-off still applies and still resets after
a successful message. `SemanticLogger.reopen(force: true)` starts a worker thread that gave up again,
which writes the messages kept on the queue. It carries on with the count of failed retries: one
that gave up after all `async_max_retries` gives up again at its first failure while the destination
is still unavailable, rather than hold up logging with a back-off as long again, and one that stopped
before using them all, such as after a fatal exception, has only the retries it had left. Once a
message is written, the count starts again. After a fork, the worker thread of the child process
starts counting afresh.

A flush or close does not wait out the back-offs of the worker thread, nor for each message ahead of
it to fail in turn. Submitting one ends the back-off under way, and until it has run, a message or
batch that the destination fails is discarded, and counted as `failed`, rather than written again
after a back-off. So is every message queued after that one, ahead of the flush or close, without
being written: during an outage, each would take as long to fail as the first, such as up to the
`open_timeout` (2 seconds by default) of an HTTP based appender whose server does not answer, or
longer, such as up to the `connect_timeout` (10 seconds by default) of each server of `:tcp`. Those
failures do not count towards `async_max_retries`. Once the flush or close has run, the messages
queued after it are written as usual. A flush still waits while the first message is tried, and
while a destination that takes the messages writes every one of them.

When the process exits, Semantic Logger flushes every appender. Before that flush, it tells each
appender added with `async: true` or in batches that the process is exiting, and each one then acts
as though a flush were already waiting: it stops backing off and writing again what failed, and once
a write fails because of its destination, discards and counts the rest of its queue, without sending
it. Each one is told directly, rather than through the queue of the thread that writes to every
appender, since that thread can be held up handing a message to the full queue of an appender that
is backing off, and so would reach the flush only once that appender stopped backing off. So during
an outage the process exits within seconds, the time one write takes to fail, rather than minutes or
hours, and an appender whose destination takes the messages still writes every one of them. A
`SemanticLogger.flush` called while the process runs reaches each appender through that thread,
behind the messages logged before it.

An appender added without `async: true`, and not in batches, such as a plain `:http`,
`:splunk_http`, `:tcp`, or `:udp`, has no queue of its own: the thread that writes to every
appender writes each message to it in turn, and carries on with the next one when it fails, without
backing off. So during an outage, the flush at exit would wait while each message queued ahead of
it failed in turn, up to the `read_timeout` or `open_timeout` of an HTTP based appender whose server
does not answer. While the process exits, once a write to such an appender fails because of its
destination, rather than the content of the message, it is given no more messages for the rest of
the flush at exit. The messages it was not given are discarded, and the flush at exit reports their
number to the internal logger, with the error, as
`Discarded 29 log message(s) during the flush at exit, after the destination failed, for appender: SemanticLogger::Appender::Http`.
The flush at exit then still flushes it, so that it delivers the messages it had already accepted,
such as those that the producer of a `:kafka` appender holds; for `:http`, `:tcp`, or `:udp` that
flush does nothing. The other appenders are still given every message. Such an appender has no count
of its own in `SemanticLogger.stats`, so that report is the only record of them. While the process
runs, it is given every message, as before, and so is it in a child process forked during the flush
at exit.

A flush or close is never left waiting on a worker thread that cannot answer it. When a batch cannot
be written, a flush or close taken off the queue with it still runs before the thread backs off; a
close then stops the thread instead of restarting it. If the worker thread ends without answering,
for example once it gives up, `SemanticLogger.flush` (including the flush at exit) stops waiting on
that appender.

### When every log entry must be delivered

Semantic Logger keeps the log entries it has not yet written in memory: on the queue of the thread
that writes to every appender, and on the queue of each appender added with `async: true` or in
batches. It does not store them anywhere that outlives the process. So the entries still queued are
lost when the process is killed (`kill -9`, the out of memory killer, or the `SIGKILL` that
Kubernetes and other process managers send once the grace period after `SIGTERM` runs out), or when
it ends without running `at_exit`, such as on a segmentation fault or `exit!`. An uncaught
exception, `exit`, and the default handling of `SIGTERM` still run the flush at exit, which writes
the queued entries to every destination that takes them.

During an outage of a remote destination, a flush, a close, and the flush at exit discard the
entries that destination fails, as described above, so that the process exits within seconds rather
than waiting for the outage to end. That holds for every `SemanticLogger.flush`, including one an
application or job framework calls while the process runs. There is no option to wait for every
entry instead: such a process would not stop until the destination came back, or until it was
killed, losing the entries anyway.

When every entry must reach its destination, such as for an audit log, write it to a local file
before the log call returns, and let a separate process deliver it:

- Log in synchronous mode (see [Synchronous operation](#synchronous-operation)), so that each entry
  is written to the file before the log call returns, rather than waiting on a queue. The file
  appender hands each entry to the operating system straight away, though without `fsync`, so a
  crash of the host itself can still lose the last entries. A write that fails, such as on a full
  disk, is reported to the internal logger rather than raised, so the log call still returns.
- In synchronous mode every appender writes on the application's thread, so add any remote appender,
  such as `:http` or `:splunk_http`, with `async: true` or in batches, or during its outage every log
  call waits out its timeouts.
- Ship the file with a log collector, such as [Vector](https://vector.dev),
  [Fluent Bit](https://fluentbit.io), or the
  [OpenTelemetry Collector](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/collector/), which keep their place in the
  file and retry until the destination accepts the entries.

~~~ruby
# Each entry is in the file before the log call returns...
SemanticLogger.sync!
SemanticLogger.add_appender(file_name: "log/production.json", formatter: :json)
# A remote appender in synchronous mode gets a thread of its own:
SemanticLogger.add_appender(appender: :http, url: "https://logs.example.com", async: true)

# ...and a collector running beside the application, such as Vector or Fluent Bit, reads the file
# and delivers every entry to the remote service, retrying through an outage.
~~~

Sending the entries to a collector or agent on the same host, such as the OpenTelemetry Collector or
Fluent Bit with its own disk buffer, narrows the window, since a connection to the same host rarely
fails, but does not close it: those entries still wait in memory, and are discarded or lost as above.

Within those limits, an appender added with `async: true` or in batches loses no entries during an
outage while the process runs and nothing flushes or closes it, until its worker thread gives up
after `async_max_retries` (see above). With `async_max_retries: -1` it never gives up, so give it a
`max_queue_size` large enough to hold the entries logged during the longest outage it should ride
out: once its queue is full, logging waits for room for as long as the outage lasts, first the
thread that writes to every appender, so that the other appenders stop receiving entries too, then
the application's log calls, once the main queue is full as well. With `non_blocking: true` on the
appender, and `SemanticLogger.non_blocking = true` for the main queue, the entries are dropped
instead (see [Drop messages instead of blocking](#drop-messages-instead-of-blocking)).

### Give a slow appender its own thread

If one destination is slow, such as a remote HTTP service, run just that appender on its own thread
and queue so it cannot hold up the others:

~~~ruby
SemanticLogger.add_appender(appender: :http, url: "https://example.com/log", async: true)
~~~

### Monitoring the background thread

The background thread can occasionally fall behind, for example when an appender is slow or a sudden
burst of logging occurs. Check the queue at runtime:

~~~ruby
# Number of log entries still waiting to be written
SemanticLogger.queue_size
~~~

In [synchronous mode](#synchronous-operation) entries are written on the calling thread, so it counts
only those logged in a signal trap that another thread has yet to write.

For a fuller operational picture, including per-appender queues, use `SemanticLogger.stats`. It
returns a Hash describing the main pipeline and every appender, handy for exporting Semantic Logger's
own health to a monitoring system such as Prometheus or statsd. A metric appender added with
`internal_metrics: true` sends the counts of the log entries processed, dropped, and failed for you
(see [Internal metrics](metrics.html#internal-metrics)).

~~~ruby
SemanticLogger.stats
# => {
#      queue_size:     0,       # entries waiting on the main pipeline queue
#      capped:         true,    # whether the main queue has a maximum size
#      max_queue_size: 10_000,  # nil when uncapped
#      thread_active:  true,    # whether the main pipeline thread is running
#      processed:      1_532,   # cumulative entries processed since startup
#      dropped:        0,       # cumulative entries dropped at the main queue
#      appenders: [
#        { name: "SemanticLogger::Appender::File", async: false },
#        { name:           "SemanticLogger::Appender::Http",
#          async:          true,    # this appender has its own thread and queue
#          thread_active:  true,
#          queue_size:     3,
#          capped:         true,
#          max_queue_size: 10_000,
#          processed:      1_529,
#          dropped:        0,
#          failed:         0 }  # discarded because they could not be written
#      ]
#    }
~~~

The `processed`, `dropped`, and `failed` counters are cumulative since process startup. Reading `stats` is
thread-safe and adds no locking to the logging hot path.

Semantic Logger also warns when an entry has waited on the queue too long. Tune the threshold and how
often it is checked:

~~~ruby
# Warn when an entry has been on the queue longer than this many seconds ( default: 30 )
SemanticLogger.lag_threshold_s

# Number of messages to process between lag checks ( default: 1,000 )
SemanticLogger.lag_check_interval = 1_000
~~~

If a sustained burst is overwhelming logging, reduce the volume by raising the log level, reduce the
number of appenders, or speed up the slow appender.

### Synchronous operation

Synchronous mode bypasses the background thread and logs inline on the calling thread. This disables
a core design principle of Semantic Logger and slows the calling thread, so it is not recommended for
most applications. It can suit short-lived or single-threaded programs, forked environments where
you would rather not re-create the logging thread, or an audit log that must be in a file before each
log call returns (see [When every log entry must be delivered](#when-every-log-entry-must-be-delivered)).

Enable it **before** adding any appenders:

~~~ruby
SemanticLogger.sync!
~~~

To guarantee it is set early enough, replace the require with the synchronous variant:

~~~ruby
require "semantic_logger/sync"
~~~

Or, in a Gemfile:

~~~ruby
gem "semantic_logger", require: "semantic_logger/sync"
~~~

In synchronous mode, one thread at a time writes to the appenders, so a log call waits while another
thread writes. Ruby does not allow that wait in a signal trap, nor an appender to lock a Mutex of its
own there, as a Ruby `Logger` given to `add_appender(logger:)` does when it writes. So a message
logged in a trap, such as by the handlers of [`add_signal_handler`](#linux-signals), is written just
after, by another thread, before any message logged after the trap; the trap does not wait for it.
That includes a trap that interrupted its own thread while it was writing a message: the trap's
message is written once that one is, never in the middle of it.

In a trap, `SemanticLogger.flush`, `close`, `reopen`, and `remove_appender` run on a thread that the
trap starts, after the messages logged in the trap before them, and the trap waits for it, at most
one second, and returns what it returned. When it has not finished by then, such as when the trap
interrupted its own thread while it was writing a message, which cannot go on before the trap
returns, the call returns `nil` and finishes just after. `add_appender` adds the appender at once.

## Linux signals

On Linux, Unix, and Mac, Semantic Logger can respond to signals, for example to change the log level
of a running process without restarting it. It registers no signal handlers on startup, so as not to
interfere with any your application already uses.

**Step 1: enable signal handling** during boot:

~~~ruby
# config/initializers/semantic_logger.rb, or during startup of a standalone app
SemanticLogger.add_signal_handler
~~~

**Step 2: send the signal** you need. The capabilities are below.

### Change the log level (USR2)

Send `SIGUSR2` to rotate the global default level, without restarting. Each signal moves the level
one step through this sequence, wrapping from `:trace` back to `:fatal`:

    :fatal  :error  :warn  :info  :debug  :trace

~~~
kill -SIGUSR2 1234
~~~

This changes only the global default level. Loggers whose level was set explicitly in the application
are unaffected.

### Dump all threads (TTIN)

Send `TTIN` to write every thread, with its backtrace where available, to the log. Naming your
threads (`Thread.current.name = "My Worker"`) makes the dump far more useful:

~~~
kill -TTIN 1234
~~~

On JRuby this differs from the standard `QUIT`-triggered Java thread dump, which includes system
threads and Java stack traces.

### JRuby garbage collection logging

On JRuby, any garbage collection that takes longer than 100ms is logged as a warning to the regular
appenders, giving visibility into GC pauses that could affect active requests.

### Choose your own signals

Pass different signals, or set one to `nil` to skip it. Set the GC threshold to `nil` to skip the
JRuby garbage collection logging:

~~~ruby
# Log level change on USR1, thread dump on USR2, GC threshold of 100,000 micro-seconds
SemanticLogger.add_signal_handler("USR1", "USR2", 100000)
~~~

## Centralized logging

Once you run more than one process or server, reading log files one at a time stops scaling. A
**centralized logging** system collects the events from every process into one place where you can
search, filter, and build dashboards across all of them at once. This is where Semantic Logger's
structured output pays off: the payload, tags, duration, and metrics on each entry arrive as real
fields, not text that has to be re-parsed.

This walks through one popular stack end to end as a concrete example:

* **Semantic Logger** forwards structured events from your application.
* **Elasticsearch** stores and indexes them.
* **Kibana** provides search and dashboards on top of Elasticsearch.

The same shape applies to other aggregators (Graylog, Splunk, Loki, Logstash, Syslog). See
[Other destinations](#other-destinations) and [Appenders](appenders.html).

### Step 1: Run Elasticsearch and Kibana

Install and start both. Any installation method works; these notes use
[homebrew](https://brew.sh) on macOS, follow the product links for other platforms.

~~~
brew install elasticsearch
brew install kibana
~~~

Start each one (follow the on-screen instructions to auto-start them), and confirm Elasticsearch is
reachable, by default at `http://localhost:9200`, and Kibana at `http://localhost:5601`.

### Step 2: Forward your application's logs

Add the Elasticsearch appender so Semantic Logger ships every entry to Elasticsearch. In a Rails app
using [rails_semantic_logger](rails.html), put this in an initializer; otherwise add it where you
configure Semantic Logger at startup:

~~~ruby
SemanticLogger.add_appender(
  appender: :elasticsearch,
  url:      "http://localhost:9200"
)
~~~

By default entries are written to a daily index named `semantic_logger-YYYY.MM.DD`, so the index
pattern to search in Kibana is `semantic_logger-*`. See [Elasticsearch](appenders.html#elasticsearch)
for options such as a custom index name or data streams.

Restart the application and exercise it so it generates a few log entries. If nothing appears later,
check the application's own log (for example `log/development.log`) for connection errors.

### Step 3: View the logs in Kibana

1. Open Kibana at [http://localhost:5601](http://localhost:5601).
2. Create an **index pattern** (called a "data view" in newer Kibana versions) that matches
   `semantic_logger-*`.
3. When asked for the time field, choose `timestamp`.
4. Open **Discover**. Your application's log entries appear. If the list is empty, widen the time
   range in the top right.
5. Add a few columns so each entry is readable at a glance, for example `host`, `level`, `name`, and
   `message`.

The exact menu names vary between Kibana versions, but the three things you need are always the same:
an index pattern of `semantic_logger-*`, a time field of `timestamp`, and the Discover view.

### Step 4: Search

In Discover, query against the structured fields directly. A few examples:

~~~
# Only error level entries
level: error

# Only entries from one host
host: mymachine

# Find a value in the logging tags
tags: 17262353
~~~

Because the payload, tags, and metrics are real fields, you can filter and build dashboards on them
without writing log-parsing expressions.

### Other destinations

Elasticsearch and Kibana are just one option. Semantic Logger also forwards to other centralized
logging systems and aggregators, including:

* Logstash
* Graylog
* Splunk
* Grafana Loki
* Loggly
* Syslog

See [Appenders](appenders.html) to configure any of these as a destination.


---

<!-- source: docs/security.md -->

## Security

Logging frameworks sit on a sensitive boundary: they take data from all over an
application, including data that originated from untrusted users, and write it to
files, terminals, and centralized logging systems. This page describes the security
properties of Semantic Logger and how to configure it when logging untrusted data.

### Log injection and forging

When a log message, tag, or exception message contains untrusted, attacker-controlled
data (for example a user name, request parameter, or `User-Agent` header), control
characters in that data can be abused:

* A newline can forge an additional, fake log entry ("log forging"), or split one
  record into two at a collector that frames records with a separator.
